items.title: AI smart glasses sold in Canada, U.S. recalled due to ‘burn hazard’
items.description: Owners of a pair of AI smart glasses sold in Canada and the U.S. are being told to 'immediately stop using' them due to a burn hazard.

items._ogDesc: Owners of a pair of AI smart glasses sold in Canada and the U.S. are being told to 'immediately stop using' them due to a burn hazard.
items.body:
Owners of a pair of AI smart glasses are being told to stop wearing them due to a burn risk.

INMO Smart Glass AIR3 glasses were recalled in both Canada and the United States this week, as the left side of the glasses may overheat during extended use, a recall notice from Heath Canada warned.

“Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and update the product firmware to version 3.16 before reusing the product,” the notice said.

The specific model can be identified by an AIR3 label found on the inside of the glasses’ right leg. The product can stream media and uses AI to assist with translation and productivity.

The glasses were sold on Amazon, Kickstarter and inmoxr.com for between US$900 and US$1300 the company said.

INMO said it sold 120 pairs of the smart glasses in Canada and 1,643 in the U.S., between December 2025 and August 2026. The recall was published jointly between Health Canada, the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission and INMO International Technology Limited.

Health Canada reported no injuries in Canada as of Sept. 17, but the U.S. notice said “the firm has received 10 reports of the AIR3 glasses overheating, including reports of a burning sensation to the face and the left side of the ear.”

INMO advises owners to contact inmoxr.com with a photo of the impacted product, along with their order number and purchase channel.

Health Canada reminded owners in their notice that “the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act prohibits recalled products from being redistributed, sold or even given away in Canada.”

items.title: Trump lays out the pomp for Xi but says little about the significant tensions in U.S.-China relations
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday hailed the “truly great friendship” he has forged with Xi Jinping as the Chinese leader began his highly anticipated state visit.

items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday hailed the “truly great friendship” he has forged with Xi Jinping as the Chinese leader began his highly anticipated state visit.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — -- Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met for high stakes talks on Thursday at an urgent moment for the U.S.-China relationship, with the world’s preeminent powers divided on the war in Iran and still grappling to find common ground on trade and how to best navigate the jarring advances of artificial intelligence.

With their countries in a generational contest for economic and technological dominance, the two appear to be betting that a combination of personal rapport and mutual interest can prevent the competition from boiling over into open conflict.

“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said as he welcomed Xi to the White House for a pomp-filled state visit.

Xi was more pointed than Trump, saying Chinese and American interests are “deeply intertwined” and that the “competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds.”

He also reiterated his warning that the U.S. and China must avoid the " Thucydides trap," referring to the idea that when a rising power threatens to displace an established one, the result is often war. Xi offered a similar warning when Trump visited Beijing in May.

“It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses,” Xi added.

China has resisted the Trump administration’s urgings -- and economic threats -- to use its considerable leverage to prod Iran to agree to U.S. terms to end the nearly seven-month war. Xi wants to see Trump permanently halt arms sales to Taiwan and loosen export restrictions on cutting-edge advanced chips. The two sides on Wednesday agreed to extend by two months a one-year trade truce that was set to expire Nov. 10 as they work to find a more durable agreement.

Xi presses Trump on Taiwan

During their private conversation on Thursday, Xi told Trump he hopes the U.S. can adhere to opposing Taiwan independence and urged him to “prudently handle the Taiwan issue,” according to the Chinese state media outlet Xinhua. The White House did not immediately release any readout of the talks and Trump, who frequently offers his own take of his interactions with foreign leaders on his social media platform, has yet to weigh in on the substance of his conversations with Xi.

Trump, who is in the midst of a legal fight after trying to bar CNN, MSNOW, and Politico from the White House, did complain that TV networks “refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years.” The White House’s five-network television pool rotation refused to cover Trump’s events in response to the action against CNN.

China has made clear it views Taiwan as the most sensitive issue in the U.S.-China relationship. Beijing considers Taiwan to be Chinese territory and vows to annex the island by force if necessary. The United States is obligated by law to provide Taiwan with sufficient hardware to deter any armed attack from the mainland. The U.S. has said it opposes any unilateral changes to the status quo by either side.

China has repeatedly pressed Washington to permanently halt the arms sales, including when Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May.

After that meeting, Trump said he was holding off on final approval for a record US$14 billion arms package that was in the pipeline. He also described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.

Xi says China and U.S. should make sure AI is `always under human control’

Trump said in a social media post earlier Thursday that artificial intelligence -- “superintelligence” as he is trying to rebrand it -- was high on the agenda. The president has been dismissive of calls for greater regulation amid growing global anxiety that the technology will kill jobs or potentially even wipe out humanity.

“I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump wrote. “That is China’s position also.”

But Xi, in his opening comments, said that the two countries had “the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people.”

The two countries’ finance ministers met earlier this week, with the U.S. proposing a new “notification mechanism” for AI incidents between the two nations.

Trump rolls out the red carpet for Xi

Trump had made clear he wanted to impress Xi with the visit. The Republican U.S. president made sure construction of a new helicopter landing pad on the White House’s South Lawn was completed before the visit and he met Xi and his wife on Wednesday evening when they flew into Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.

The White House also arranged an elaborate military review, which the leaders and their spouses observed before the Oval Office talks.

After about 90 minutes of talks, the leaders stepped out to the South Lawn so Trump could show off the new White House helipad and give Xi a tour of Marine One, the presidential helicopter. Trump and Xi also appeared to peer at the ballroom construction site from afar. Xi left the White House shortly after the quick tour and returned in the evening for the state dinner.

No Chinese CEOs at state dinner

Tech titans, including Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and Tesla and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, were among the 130 guests invited to the black-tie dinner, but Chinese CEOs were conspicuously absent.

U.S. and Chinese planners did discuss including several executives from some notable Chinese companies, according to a person familiar with the planning for the state visit who was not authorized to comment publicly.

One obstacle that came up during the negotiations for the state visits was that the U.S. side was slow to propose protocols and clarify the roles the Chinese CEOs would have during the state visit, the person said. The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the absence of Chinese business leaders.

While Trump has offered plenty of glitz, some China analysts observed that the talks seemed light on substance.

Danny Russel, a former senior U.S. State Department official who served in former U.S. president Barack Obama’s administration, observed that the two leaders spent more time in social and ceremonial events than in formal talks about the core issues facing the two nations.

“What we’re seeing isn’t diplomacy so much as `diplotainment,’ which won’t do much to solve the serious problems in the U.S.-China relationship,” said Russel, who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

Xi urges U.S. and Iran to return to interim agreement

The two sides discussed the ongoing conflict in Iran, according to Chinese state broadcaster China Central Television.

Trump has argued to little effect that China, which is far more dependent on Gulf oil than the U.S., has plenty of incentive to use its sway with Tehran to help force an end to the conflict.

But Trump’s war of choice has unnerved Beijing, with the government condemning the U.S. and Israeli military action and Xi previously expressing concerns that the conflict signaled a return to what he called the “law of the jungle.” The U.S. administration has warned China, Tehran’s biggest trading partner, not to aid Iran’s military effort.

Xi, during Thursday’s talks, said China supports the U.S. and Iran returning to a short-lived interim deal from the summer to wind down the war, according to CCTV. That agreement broke down soon after it was signed in June as the countries traded renewed fire over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for energy shipments.

By Aamer Madhani, Didi Tang and Michelle L. Price, The Associated Press

Associated Press writers Bill Barrow, Collin Binkley, Josh Boak, Kevin Freking, Seung Min Kim, Darlene Superville and Will Weissert and AP photographer Jacquelyn Martin contributed to this report.

items.title: ‘Analyzing risk scenarios’ normal, defence minister says amid Carney’s U.S. invasion comments
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney has carefully examined the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump ordering a military invasion of Canada, according to a new report.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark, left to right, a soldier of the 41 Canadian Brigade Group and Defence Minister David McGuinty in a combination photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld/Jeff McIntosh/Chad Hipolito]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney has carefully examined the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump ordering a military invasion of Canada, according to a new report.
items.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said he’s prepared for the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump ordering a military invasion of Canada, according to a new report.

In an interview with the New York Times published Wednesday, Carney described the prospect of an invasion as an “extreme tail risk,” meaning impactful though unlikely, but that it would be “irresponsible” not to prepare.

On Thursday, Defence Minister David McGuinty commented on Carney’s New York Times comments ahead of a cabinet meeting Thursday afternoon, telling reporters it’s “normal” for federal governments and militaries to analyze “risk scenarios.”

Meanwhile, Trump said on Truth Social Wednesday that “Canada is destroying itself by allowing millions and millions of people into the Country” who were “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

  • Carney called U.S. military action ‘extreme tail risk’
  • Vietnam’s leader is in Ottawa
  • Canada’s first F-35 takes flight

Here’s what happened on Sept. 24, 2026:

Carney prepared for U.S. invasion of Canada: NYT

Carney has carefully examined the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump ordering a military invasion of Canada, according to a new report.

In an interview with The New York Times released Wednesday, Carney described the prospect as an “extreme tail risk,” a term used to describe an event that could cause enormous damage, but is very unlikely.

However, the prime minister explained that what he did was “just risk management.”

“That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare for the possibility, Carney told The Times.

Tammy Ibrahimpoor, CTVNews.ca producer

‘Normal’ for feds to analyze ‘risk scenarios’: defence minister

Defence Minister David McGuinty commented on Carney’s New York Times comments ahead of a cabinet meeting Thursday afternoon, telling reporters it’s “normal” for federal governments and militaries to analyze “risk scenarios.”

The comments come after Carney’s New York Times’ story, in which he said he studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada.

“We’re talking about all kinds of issues around keeping North America safe, and that’s exactly what we’re doing,” McGuinty said.

“It is normal. All militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios.”

Pressed for details on what specific risk scenarios were assessed, McGuinty would not clarify.

“The prime minister also indicated that that’s the kind of detail that we would not get into. We won’t get into that,” McGuinty said.

Stephanie Ha, CTVNews.ca, ONB manager

It’s ‘prudent’ to run ‘any scenario’: AI minister

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon was asked Thursday by CTV News chief political correspondent Vassy Kapelos to comment on Carney’s remarks that “it would be irresponsible” not to prepare for the possibility of a U.S. invasion.

Solomon responded by saying it is “prudent to run any scenario.”

“That’s the way every government functions. You run any scenario, so you’re prepared for everything. This is not abnormal to think of whatever the long-term risks of any scenario is,” he said.

But pressed by Kapelos on what those preparations could look like, Solomon would not answer directly.

“I’m not going to get into how the military prepares for any scenario,” he said.

Stephanie Ha, CTVNews.ca, ONB manager

Carney NYT comments not ‘in our favour’

Peter MacKay, former defence and foreign affairs minister, called it irresponsible for Carney to discuss preparing for a potential U.S. invasion in comments published Wednesday in The New York Times.

MacKay told CTV News Channel on Thursday, that he was confused by the prime minister’s comments which he said “takes us from the realm of retaliation to provocation.”

“What we really need to do, in my humble opinion, is to get back to the bargaining table and talk about the removal of tariffs,” he added.

MacKay said he does not understand Carney’s rationale for going down that road, “especially when tensions are so high.”

“I’m not sure what the effort was here, to perhaps play to a domestic audience, to send a message to the White House, but I don’t think it’s working in our favour.”

Joe Van Wonderen, CTVNews.ca journalist

Carney meets Vietnam leader

Carney says there will be “good news” coming for people who want to travel from Canada to Vietnam, without providing details.

Vietnamese President Tô Lâm is in Ottawa today for a meeting with the prime minister. In brief remarks Thursday, Carney said the two leaders were working on a new agreement on “people-to-people ties,” as well as energy, agriculture, and defence co-operation.

Vietnam is Canada’s largest trading partner in the Southeast Asian bloc ASEAN. Canada exported $1.3 billion in merchandise to Vietnam last year and imported $19.3 billion.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada’s first F-35 takes flight

Canada’s first F-35 has taken to the skies. It’s the first new model of fighter jet with Canadian markings in 44 years. But a milestone that would normally be heavily promoted, passed with barely a word from Canada’s military.

The historic first flight took place Wednesday in Fort Worth, Texas, home to Lockheed Martin’s final assembly plant.

The low-key debut comes as Ottawa’s review of the F-35 purchase continues. Canada signed on in 2023 to buy 88 of the jets, but Carney ordered a review in March 2025 amid tensions with the United States.

Canada’s first F-35s will be used to train RCAF pilots in the U.S. at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona. The first jets are expected to arrive in Canada in 2028, with initial operational capability in 2029.

John Vennavally-Rao, CTV News national correspondent. Read the full story here.

Times reporter on Carney interview

Carney paused for several seconds after the Times asked him about Canada’s preparations for U.S. military action.

He “clearly reflected very, very carefully on what he wanted to say,” said the newspaper’s Canada Bureau Chief Matina Stevis-Gridneff, the article’s lead reporter.

When Carney said he had examined it out of a sense of responsibility, “I think everyone around the table understood what he meant,” Stevis-Gridneff told CTV Your Morning.

She and her colleagues asked him for specifics on what sort of actions Canada had taken to prepare, but Carney refused to do so, Stevis-Gridneff also said.

“He did not use the word ‘invasion’ to be clear, that was our word.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Risk management plan is ‘prudent’

CTV News U.S. political analyst Eric Ham said Carney was being “prudent” in considering the unlikely scenario of the U.S. taking military action against Canada.

“We know what the United States has done in Venezuela,” Ham said from Washington, adding that tensions around U.S. control of Greenland also grew to a fever pitch earlier this year.

  • U.S.-Denmark military pact welcomed cautiously by Greenland

Tom Mulcair, another political analyst and former leader of the federal NDP, said risk management of this kind is part of the job for a prime minister.

“It’s not because someone imagined it in some vague committee on Parliament Hill in Ottawa. It’s because Donald Trump said he was going to try to make Canada the 51st state.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump has called Canada action ‘highly unlikely’

Back in May 2025, Trump was asked if he would consider sending the military into Canada.

“I think we’re not going to ever get to that point,” Trump told CBS News.

“Something could happen with Greenland. I’ll be honest, we need that for national and international security.”

“But I think it’s highly unlikely,” he also said. “I don’t see it with Canada. I just don’t see it, I have to be honest with you.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada aims to reduce reliance on U.S.: Carney

In the interview with The New York Times, Carney said Canada was looking into expanding its economic ties with China and reducing both its military and technological reliance on the United States, including Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite systems.

The prime minister also told the Times that in the future, with a different U.S. president, “we will be a better partner for the U.S. because of what we are doing.”

Tammy Ibrahimpoor, CTVNews.ca producer

Canada still reviewing F-35 fighter jet order: Carney

The prime minister also discussed Canada’s review of its planned order of 88 U.S. F-35 fighter jets, and the potential of instead buying Sweden’s Saab Gripen fighters.

“It is a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies, and because of the economic return,” Carney said.

Canada has already committed to buying 16 of the American F-35 fighter jets to replace the country’s aging fleet of CF-18 Hornets, but Carney ordered a review of the contract for the remaining 72 aircraft after Trump first announced tariffs on Canadian goods early last year.

Earlier this month, Defence Minister David McGuinty said Ottawa was assessing all available options.

Tammy Ibrahimpoor, CTVNews.ca producer

With files from Todd Coyne, CTVNewsVancouver.ca journalist

Would Carney run again?

In a separate article published by the New York Times, the prime minister also shed light on some domestic political questions.

Of note, Carney indicated he’s considering running for a second term, if the work he’s doing during his first is not complete, according to the newspaper.

“It’s too early to start asking” he said, referencing whether he would run again. “My value as a member of my party is to hit on the big things and move forward. And then, at the end of that, you see how much has got done, and if something else needs to be done.”

The prime minister, noting he has a majority government, said he’s aware a lot of what he’s committed to will take another year and a half to two years to yield results Canadians would feel, such as the development of major infrastructure and energy projects. His description of this was that it would be “beyond” the current political cycle.

Rachel Aiello, CTV News Ottawa Bureau correspondent

Judge orders access for news outlets

A federal judge temporarily blocked Trump’s ban of three news outlets from the White House, ordering early Thursday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored. Reporters from all three outlets, however, said they remained blocked a few hours after the ruling.

The back-and-forth is the latest in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes.

Trump first announced he was banning the outlets Friday, assailing what he called “fake news,” and only later arguing that their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets argued in a joint lawsuit that the ban was a blatant violation of the First Amendment because it singled them out for the content of their coverage.

In his late-night ruling, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the three outlets’ access.

The Associated Press

Reporters still without access

Reporters for CNN, MS NOW and Politico said they were still blocked early Thursday, a few hours after the order was made.

The Associated Press

Here’s what happened on Sept. 23, 2026:

Canada ‘destroying itself’

Trump says, “Canada is destroying itself by allowing millions and millions of people into the Country.”

He made the statement on his Truth Social platform Wednesday morning, accusing Canada of allowing people in who are “essentially unchecked and unvetted” and ”causing problems that will soon be too big to handle.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump talks Canadian unemployment

In Trump’s post, he mentioned what he called Canada’s “big” unemployment rate.

“It is a Liberal takeover that will end up very badly,” he said. “Already showing up in their numbers. Big unemployment.”

Canada’s unemployment rate was 6.4 per cent in August, according to the most recent labour survey from Statistics Canada.

That’s more than two percentage points above the U.S. reported unemployment rate, which was 4.1 per cent in August. However, the two countries calculate unemployment differently. For example, Canada considers people who are not working because of family responsibilities as unemployed, but the U.S. does not.

A TD study released in the fall of 2025 predicted the unemployment rate would have been at least one point higher if population growth had not been slowed.

Unemployment is impacted by a number of factors, not limited to immigration. For example, Statistics Canada noted accelerated employment losses in trade-dependent industries following Trump’s imposition of tariffs on Canadian goods.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Data contradict Trump immigration claims

As U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada is “destroying itself” with its immigration policies, new data from Statistics Canada show the number of newcomers is going down.

According to Statistics Canada, Canada’s population rose slightly by 0.2 per cent in the second quarter, while immigration is down 4.2 per cent year-over-year, and the number of non-permanent residents is down 0.7 per cent.

The Canadian government under former prime minister Justin Trudeau pledged to cut its immigration targets following years of criticism that they were putting too much pressure on the housing market and other sectors.

In Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first budget in late 2025, the Liberals set new targets, promising to “responsibly manage immigration to alleviate pressures on housing demand.”

Immigration levels in Canada reached a record high in 2024. According to the federal government, 483,640 immigrants were admitted as permanent residents that year, which was in line with targets set out in the Government of Canada’s Immigration Levels Plan at the time. In 2025, that number dropped to about 393,500 new permanent residents.

Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer

Anand responds to Trump

Asked to respond to Trump’s comments, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said that, while immigration overall has improved “Canadian prosperity,” the federal government reduced immigration intake in 2024.

“We are stabilizing immigration levels,” she said Wednesday, adding Ottawa moved to reduce levels to ensure accessibility to affordable housing and health care.

Canada plans to reduce temporary resident volumes to five per cent by the end of 2027.

Overall permanent resident admissions are projected to stabilize at 380,000 from 2026 to 2028, with a preference on offering status to migrants who are already in Canada with “needed skills and experience.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

No more Trump Avenue

A street in Canada’s capital bearing the name of the current U.S. president will be renamed.

Ottawa city council unanimously agreed to a motion to begin the process of renaming Trump Avenue, in Ottawa’s Central Park neighbourhood.

Trump Avenue is one of several streets in Central Park that references New York City. Other street names include Madison Park, Manhattan Crescent, Bloomingdale Street, and Staten Street.

At the time of the neighbourhood’s development, Trump was a famous real estate mogul, but his tumultuous time as president of the United States has led to renewed calls to take his name off street signs in the capital.

Ted Raymond, CTVNewsOttawa.ca journalist.

Read the full story here

Carney talks bilateral collaboration

Carney, who is co-hosting the OceanEye event, says the meeting is in the same spirit as his trip to Strasbourg last week, where talk of Canada’s associate EU membership made headlines worldwide.

Today, he said, is all about what “nations coming together” can accomplish. He did not mention the United States in his opening remarks.

He said Canada is committing $82 million to the ocean observation program, which he characterized as an imperative step for the country with the world’s longest coastline.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada to protect more lands and waters

Carney said Canada plans to send autonomous underwater gliders on months-long assignments to monitor activity under the Arctic ice.

“We can’t protect what we can’t see,” he said, adding Ottawa plans to expand protected lands and waters to two-million-square kilometres by the end of the decade.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Carney to appear with EU leader

Carney will speak at the OceanEye International Alliance event at 10 a.m. EDT. The OceanEye initiative aims to build capacity for marine observance, which the European Commission says is associated with a market worth up to C$32 billion.

“This serves a much larger business ecosystem worth EUR 40 to 90 billion, in which the United States holds the largest share,” reads a statement from the commission published earlier this year.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist. Read the full story here.

Diana Fox Carney is Canada’s Ocean Envoy

Diana Fox Carney, who’s married to Mark Carney, is Canada’s Ocean Envoy. She was named to the unpaid position in mid-September.

“In this role, Mme. Fox Carney will advance Canada’s leadership by connecting ocean conservation, climate action, Indigenous leadership, economic resilience and maritime security,” reads a release announcing her appointment.

Fox Carney, an economist and sustainability advisor, holds master’s degrees in agricultural economics from the University of Oxford and in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Here’s what happened on Sept. 22, 2026:

India’s Modi to visit Canada: Carney

Carney confirmed on Tuesday that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be visiting Canada in December.

The news was first reported by the Globe and Mail on Tuesday, citing India’s High Commissioner to Canada, who says Modi will be visiting to sign a trade deal between the two countries.

“We are making good progress in our trade negotiations with India,” Carney said, before confirming Modi’s mid-December visit to Canada.

“It is an exceptionally important relationship on many, many levels.”

Modi’s last trip to Canada was in June 2025, when he attended the G7 Summit in Kananaskis, Alta.

The visit raised eyebrows at the time because of the previously strained relationship between Canada and India.

The two countries had been at odds since 2023, when the federal government first levelled allegations of both foreign interference and transnational repression, including crimes such as murder and extortion.

At the time, talks toward a free-trade agreement — which had been underway for years — were indefinitely put on pause, and not picked up again until Carney became prime minister.

Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer

Carney reacts to Trump’s Belarus potash deal

Carney touched on Canada’s potash industry, after Trump revealed on Monday that the U.S. plans to buy cheaper product from Belarus.

“My message to the Canadian potash industry is one of admiration,” Carney said to reporters at the UN. “Canada supplies 40 per cent of the world’s potash. It is an incredible strength of our economy.”

Carney affirmed that Canadian potash would continue to be in demand around the world due to Canada being a reliable, cost-competitive supplier.

The prime minister also said Canada will continue to be the largest supplier of potash to the U.S. and expressed that now is an opportunity for Canada and its neighbours to co-operate and “become fertilizer independent.”

“So not just potash, but across all ammonia and other fertilizers, that would be good for Canadian farmers,” he said.

“It’d be great for American farmers, and it’s an opportunity we’re prepared to explore.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

U.S. to continue buying Canadian potash: Trump

Trump says his country will continue buying Canadian potash after all.

Trump made the comments to reporters during a bilateral meeting at the United Nations General Assembly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“Belarus has a lot of potash, and our farmers need good prices, and we want to get a lower price,” Trump told reporters Tuesday when asked about the proposed deal.

“We’ll continue to go with Canada, but Belarus would like to sell it for a much lower price.”

The Canadian Press. Read the full article here.

items.title: AI arms race takes centre stage as Chinese President Xi and Trump meet
items.description: As Xi Jinping arrived at the White House, no amount of diplomatic pageantry could hide the fact that China and the U.S. are competing in an arms race towards global AI dominance.

items._ogDesc: As Xi Jinping arrived at the White House, no amount of diplomatic pageantry could hide the fact that China and the U.S. are competing in an arms race towards global AI dominance.
items.body:
TORONTO - As Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived at the White House on Thursday, no amount of diplomatic pageantry could hide the fact that China and the United States are competing in an arms race towards global artificial intelligence dominance.

Ahead of the meeting with Xi, U.S. President Donald Trump took to Truth Social to indicate once again that he’s opposed to any international framework that would put up safeguards around the development of artificial intelligence.

“Big day with President Xi of China. Super Intelligence will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!” he posted.

However, there are growing concerns being shared about the potential for catastrophic risks if safeguards are not put in place to protect humanity from an AI takeover.

The Godfather of AI, Canadian Geoffrey Hinton, says the concerns are far reaching.

“There’s a risk of bad actors abusing AI for things like cyber attacks or making biological weapons, some terrorists already have the capability of building biological weapons thanks to AI.”

Just this week, Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed that an OpenAI autonomous agent “infiltrated” the countries health-care system, which is believed by experts to be a world first.

At a UN Security Council meeting in New York on Wednesday, Sam Altman CEO of OpenAI, conceded that regulations are needed.

“It doesn’t matter if people put the level of catastrophe at 10 per cent or 1 per cent or 12 per cent or 0.1 per cent. None of these levels are remotely acceptable,” said Altman.

The co-founder of Anthropic shared a similar concerning message with the UN Security Council. Dario Amodei called the rapid, unchecked pace of AI development “the most important global security issue facing the world today.”

Amodei also warning that without a slowdown in development, AI could be capable of leading a swarm of autonomous agents that could “take over the entire internet” within six to 12 months.

Earlier this month, Trump emphasized his belief that falling behind China in the AI race simply is not an option.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins. And we can put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up,” Trump said.

The two countries are leading in AI, though which country is winning the race is less clear. Trump has openly shared his view that China is America’s main rival.

Hinton says regardless of the desire to build fast, AI leaders must also build with intention.

“Instead of just racing to make AI smarter and smarter, we should be racing to make it into a better kind of being. We’re creating beings for the first time, these things really understand what they’re saying, they really have intentions,” shares Hinton.

items.title: Bonnie Crombie wants to extend the Line 2 subway into Mississauga
items.description: Mississauga mayoral candidate Bonnie Crombie says “it is time” to extend the TTC’s Line 2 subway “into the heart of Mississauga.”
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Ontario Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie speaks after winning 57 per cent of the vote in a leadership review at the Ontario Liberal Party annual general meeting on Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Mississauga mayoral candidate Bonnie Crombie says “it is time” to extend the TTC’s Line 2 subway “into the heart of Mississauga.”
items.body:
Mississauga mayoral candidate Bonnie Crombie says “it is time” to extend the TTC’s Line 2 subway “into the heart of Mississauga.”

In a news release issued this week, Crombie unveiled a transportation plan dubbed “Mississauga Moves 2.0.”

The centrepiece of the plan is a proposed extension of Line 2 into Mississauga, which she says would create a direct subway connection between the city and Toronto’s existing transit network.

“The long-term objective is to extend the Toronto Transit Commission’s Line 2 west from Kipling, serve Sherway Gardens and continue into the heart of Mississauga, creating a direct connection between the city and Toronto’s subway network,” she said in a news release.

If elected, Crombie says that in her first year as mayor, she would seek a formal partnership with Ontario, Metrolinx, the City of Toronto and the TTC to launch a business case study examining potential routes, station locations, ridership and construction options.

The study would also look at the possibility of running the subway above-ground along parts of the Dundas Street corridor rather than assuming the entire extension would have to be underground.

“Vaughan is on the subway map. Scarborough is getting a major subway extension... Mississauga should be part of that conversation too,” Crombie added.

She also plans to connect the subway extension with other existing and planned rapid transit projects, including the Hazel McCallion Line, Mississauga Transitway and MiWay.

The Hazel McCallion Line is another major focus of the plan. Crombie is calling for the line to open to passengers “no later than” by Dec. 31, 2028.

“Within the first 100 days of the next Council term, the City should ask Metrolinx and Ontario to publish a transparent milestone schedule showing what remains to be completed, when testing will begin and what needs to happen before passengers can board,” she added.

Beyond the LRT, Crombie is proposing 15-minute-or-better all-day service on major MiWay corridors and 10-minute-or-better service on the busiest routes where ridership supports it.

She is also proposing an Airport Workforce Transit Network connecting to Pearson International Airport, adding that the service would be designed around the early mornings, late evenings, weekends and shift changes of airport workers.

When it comes to roads, Crombie is proposing a “Traffic Flow First” program that would “synchronize traffic signals,” and expand adaptive signal technology. She says it’s an effort to get “more capacity and reliability out of the infrastructure the city already has.”

The plan would also include stronger enforcement against vehicles and construction activity blocking travel lanes during peak periods, as well as an annual congestion report card tracking travel times, delays, transit reliability and construction impacts.

“The purpose of better transit is partly to give more people an alternative so fewer vehicles are competing for the same road space,” Crombie said.

Alvin Tedjo: ‘A step behind’

In an email to CTV News, Alvin Tedjo’s campaign acknowledged that Mississauga residents deserve quick, reliable and affordable transit, but noted that a strong relationship with the province should be the “first step.”

“While a subway extension may be a dream worth pursuing, the first step for any Mayor is building a strong working relationship with the province to secure the support and funding needed to make it happen. And the candidate proposing this idea is already a step behind,” the statement read.

Dipika Damerla: Upgrading Lakeshore GO line

Speaking to CTV News, candidate Dipika Damerla revealed that she is calling for the existing Lake Shore GO line to be converted into a de facto surface subway by adding more stations in Mississauga.

She explained that rather than relying solely on new subway or LRT projects, residents would benefit from a “cheaper, faster, and less disruptive” upgrade than any other plan on the table.

“Last time when I ran, I did propose a subway expansion into Mississauga, and I still do,” she said. “I want to convert the Lake Shore GO line that we have into a surface subway by adding more transit stops in Mississauga...that’s where we really need it right now.”

The 2026 municipal election will be held on Oct. 26.

items.description: With a wrench in hand, second-year Electric Vehicle Technician students at Ontario’s Durham College are hoping that all their hard work will help them fasten their future career choice.

items._ogDesc: With a wrench in hand, second-year Electric Vehicle Technician students at Ontario’s Durham College are hoping that all their hard work will help them fasten their future career choice.
items.body:
WHITBY, Ont. - With a wrench in hand, second-year Electric Vehicle Technician students at Ontario’s Durham College are hoping that all their hard work will help them fasten their future career choice.

The program is only in its second year, though its gaining plenty of buzz around campus and enrollment demand has risen year over year.

“It’s the direction that everything is going,” proclaims Durham College Hybrid Electric Vehicle Professor, Mike Frederick.

The Federal Government expects to reach a 75 per cent electric vehicle (EV) adoption rate by 2035, with hopes of reaching a goal 90 per cent by 2040.

“As an automotive technician, if we can’t repair EV’s there’s going to be serious consequences. There’s going to be increased demand for all automotive technicians in the near future, there’s more people retiring from the industry than graduates coming into the industry right now” says Frederick.

He tells CTV News he believes automotive technicians are just one of multiple trades soon to be in high demand across Canada.

“I believe the average age of a bricklayer right now is 59 years old, all of the old trades guys like me are starting to get out of it,” adds Frederick.

According to the federal government, by 2033, Canada will need more than 1.4 million new trades workers across the country, in-part due to a retirement rate of trades workers that’s sitting at about 21 per cent.

“With the number of people reaching their retirement age we do need to backfill all those jobs and if you look at anything happening with construction, anything happening in Ontario, or elsewhere in the country, we need trades workers, we need skilled professionals,” says Durham College Skilled Trades Associate Dean, Kara Woods.

The most recent data from Statistics Canada backs up the claim made by both Woods and Frederick. Stats Can says roughly 700,000 tradespeople are expected to retire by the end of this decade.

Trades as a viable career path

“I’m trying to follow the future that’s going to come” says second-year Electric Vehicle Technician student, Noman Shakeel.

Shakeel moved from Pakistan to Canada 20 years ago. For the larger part of the two decades, he was running a restaurant and working as a chef, until the pandemic hit and he watched as the spending habits of Canadians changed.

The second-year student believes working in the trades and specifically training to be an EV technician, will position him well in a future job market that’s become difficult to predict with the rise of AI technology.

“When it comes to working with electric vehicles, you’re not only looking into the EV industry, but you also have electric lawnmowers at home, delivery trucks you see on the road, trains and the wider transport sector, I have a whole field of industry right in front of me that needs workers,” says Shakeel.

Canadian families are increasingly looking at the trades as a viable option for their children, with one report finding that half of Canadians now see trade school as the best way to prepare their child for a career by 2050, compared to just 37 per cent feeling the same way about a university degree.

“Building Canada,” has been a buzz term shared by the federal government. As part of the Federal Governments “Team Canada Strong” initiative, Ottawa has pledged $8 billion to recruit and train up to 100,000 new red-seal trades workers within the next five years.

“If you want to build a country, you need to get into the trades, you need to have the hands-on skills. The power of any nation is its ability to build their own industries, rather than getting it from somewhere else,” says Shakeel.

As Shakeel packs his school bag and heads to his next class for the day, the second-year college student shares that one day he hopes to have his own hybrid and electric vehicle mechanic shop. He believes it’s a dream that he’ll soon make a reality.

items.title: Businesses should prepare for new Canada-U.S. relationship: former diplomat
items.description: Canada’s former ambassador to the United States is urging Canadian business leaders to prepare for a lasting shift in the country’s economic relationship with its largest trading partner, rather than assuming things will eventually return to the way they were.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Kirsten Hillman speaks to media in Philadelphia on Tuesday, May 21, 2024.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Canada’s former ambassador to the United States is urging Canadian business leaders to prepare for a lasting shift in the country’s economic relationship with its largest trading partner, rather than assuming things will eventually return to the way they were.
items.body:
Canada’s former ambassador to the United States is urging Canadian business leaders to prepare for a lasting shift in the country’s economic relationship with its largest trading partner, rather than assuming things will eventually return to the way they were.

“I think we need to find a new path,” said Kirsten Hillman in Banff, Alta., on Thursday.

Her remarks came on the opening day of the 27th annual Global Business Forum, which is taking place Thursday and Friday at the Fairmont Banff Springs.

This year’s theme is “Thriving in Chaos,” with speakers discussing global business, politics, security and other issues facing the international community.

Hillman, who served as Canada’s ambassador to the U.S. from 2020 until earlier this year, said Canadian companies need to recognize the assumptions underpinning decades of deeply integrated Canada-U.S. trade have changed.

“We have taken for granted that we would have virtually duty-free trade with the United States and a sense of mutual commitment to building deeply integrated economies,” she said.

“If CEOs are not paying attention to that and recognizing that, then it could be their sector next, it could happen to them as well,” she said.

The warning comes as trade talks between Canada and the U.S. remain stalled after negotiations broke in August. Escalating tariff measures from both countries have since ensued.

The two countries remain deeply economically connected, but Hillman described the current tensions as part of a broader change in how the U.S. views its relationship with Canada.

“It is not about a specific sector. It is about a change in perspective and philosophy, or the revelation of a perspective and philosophy that’s probably always been there and is now being actualized through President Trump and his team and his vision,” she said.

For Canadian businesses, that means looking beyond the U.S. market and building greater resilience at home.

“One customer is not a very resilient way to be,” Hillman said.

She encouraged companies to take advantage of opportunities to increase domestic sales, strengthen the Canadian market and diversify their customer base.

The shift could also prompt Canada to become more self-reliant, while changing how the country approaches its relationship with its southern neighbour.

Canadians, Hillman said, have traditionally viewed the relationship through the lens of partnership, often seeing Canada as a supportive junior partner to the U.S.

“I think that Canadians have this sense of sort of the wingman, right, and that we’re there, and we’re going to be the best junior partner that you’ve got to help do all your stuff,” she said.

The American perspective, however, places greater emphasis on national interests.

“Ultimately, Americans understand their own sense of fighting for their country, being American, being patriotic, doing things for themselves, doing things for their country and their individual interest within that context,” she said.

Hillman added that Canadians are now gaining a better understanding of that perspective, which could push the country to make progress on issues that have been discussed for years.

She pointed to interprovincial trade, major infrastructure projects and energy development.

“We’ve been talking about this for generations, but we haven’t, or at least not our generation, and we haven’t done it, and now we are going to do it.”

Greater self-reliance, she added, doesn’t necessarily mean moving away from the United States.

Instead, Canada could approach the relationship from a different position and make more deliberate decisions about where deeper economic integration makes sense.

“I think understanding that and taking a bit of that attitude ourselves is going to make us a stronger country,” Hillman said.

She expects Canada and the U.S. to remain close partners but said the relationship could be stronger if Canadians approach it with a clearer understanding of their own interests.

items.title: Vietnam's leader To Lam visits Ottawa as Carney reaches out to middle powers
items.description: Vietnam’s most powerful politician is in Ottawa for a state visit Thursday aimed at deepening trade and diplomatic ties as middle powers confront American and Chinese coercion.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Vietnam's President To Lam arrives to attend the International Space Summit in Paris Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (Abdul Saboor/Pool Photo via AP)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Abdul Saboor</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Vietnam’s most powerful politician is in Ottawa for a state visit Thursday aimed at deepening trade and diplomatic ties as middle powers confront American and Chinese coercion.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Vietnamese President To Lam has upgraded ties with Canada to a strategic partnership, building on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to get middle powers working more closely together to confront American and Chinese coercion.

“In a volatile world, trust, responsibility and shared interests in and of themselves are strategic values,” Lam said Thursday through an interpreter in an address on Parliament Hill.

His one-day state visit involved numerous events, including a tree-planting at Rideau Hall and an address to parliamentarians and members of the diaspora.

Lam is the first Vietnamese president ever to visit Canada and he leads the country’s communist party, making him its most powerful person.

In a meeting in Carney’s West Block office, the prime minister commended Lam for his leadership of a middle power and said the relationship has evolved quickly since a 2017 pact that covered investment, defence and academia.

“There will be good news for those who want to travel directly from Canada to Vietnam and back,” Carney said, possibly suggesting direct commercial flights.

The new strategic partnership signifies deeper co-operation on longer-term goals, said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a geopolitics think tank.

“We’re in a moment where the relationship can go to a new level, and there’s definitely political desire on both sides.”

Nadjibulla said that while Vietnam is a communist country, it’s also trade-dependent — like Canada — and seeks to preserve the rules-based international order and pursue economic diversification.

“Even though its leadership is very different from Canada, its orientation right now is very much similar to what Canada is trying to do, which is build resilience, diversify partnerships and practise as much autonomy and agency (so as) not to be coerced by any one power,” she said.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said the renewed partnership will involve energy, agriculture, defence co-operation and people-to-people ties. She said Canadian universities and investors can help Vietnam as it shifts from economic development toward an innovation economy.

“As the global economy changes, our response is not to turn inward. It is to build partnerships,” she said.

Lam said those partnerships should span Canadian technology, particularly in agriculture, clean energy and education.

“We need to maintain regular exchanges and contacts, especially at the high level at an early stage — and in a frank manner — on the shifts that may affect the interests of each side,” he said.

Lam called for “tangible action programs with clearcut priorities” that will help eliminate “bottlenecks.”

Global Affairs Canada’s online profile of Vietnam calls it Canada’s largest trading partner in Southeast Asia, with two-way merchandise trade amounting to more than $20 billion last year. Canada exports food, metals and fertilizers, while Vietnam exports electronics, clothing, furniture and shoes.

“Vietnam is an economic partner that plays an important role in advancing Canada’s trade diversification efforts in the region,” the department says.

Vietnam is also a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a bloc with which Canada is negotiating a free-trade agreement. Carney is hoping to sign that trade agreement on a planned November visit to the Philippines — which might include a stop in Vietnam.

Nadjibulla said Vietnam has a huge trade surplus with multiple countries, including Canada, in part because U.S. President Donald Trump used his first term to promote trade with Asian nations other than China. That led to a boom in Vietnamese electronics manufacturing.

“We import a lot from Vietnam and we sell very little, relatively speaking,” she said, arguing Canadian businesses have not seized opportunities in this country of 100 million people.

Vietnam is now facing hefty American tariffs and is working on a bilateral agreement with Washington while trying to diversify its trade beyond the U.S.

“This is where Canada and Vietnam are aligned. We’re both trying to diversify our supply chains (and) reduce overreliance on the U.S.,” Nadjibulla said.

Vietnam is also at the forefront of American efforts to weed out forced labour from supply chains, especially supply chains that could be linked to Uyghur slave labour in China’s Xinjiang region.

Canada’s former corporate ombudsperson raised similar concerns about running shoes produced in Vietnam, warning they might include cotton derived from slave labour.

Beijing calls the Trump administration’s claims about slave labour unfounded and says they’re aimed at undercutting China’s economic growth. Vietnam has said it takes Washington’s concerns seriously.

This year, Vietnam holds the rotating chairmanship of the Pacific Rim trade bloc known as CPTPP. The bloc brings together multiple countries, including Canada, Chile, Japan and Australia, which commit to rules-based commerce and basic workers’ rights.

The CPTPP bloc has taken on increasing importance as countries deal with acts of economic coercion — such as China limiting supply chains for critical minerals and Trump issuing tariffs on questionable grounds.

Lam has been supportive of Carney’s fledgling initiative to have the European Union work more with the CPTPP bloc so that middle powers can band together against coercive policies.

“It has made the relationship even more significant this year, because of that international agenda,” Nadjibulla said.

The opening of a massive Volkswagen electric vehicle battery plant in southwestern Ontario has been pushed back two years until 2029.

PowerCo Canada, a subsidiary of the German automaker, says it is delaying production at the $7-billion factory in St. Thomas, Ont., in order to align the project’s timeline and product strategy with evolving market demand, technological advancements and the Volkswagen Group’s long-term strategy.

It says the later opening date will allow for next-generation battery technology while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve.

Joel Karlsberg, chief procurement officer for the battery company, says the move is “about getting the pacing right ... to protect our long-term investment (and) support regional jobs.”

PowerCo also announced Thursday it has selected Canadian construction firm EllisDon Corp. as general contractor for construction of the factory as it moves into its next phase, which will focus on core infrastructure and structural work.

The plant was announced in 2023, with the federal government committing $700 million in upfront capital costs to build the factory and Ontario kicking in $500 million.

items.title: 7 in 10 B.C. newcomers who don't own homes intend to buy one: survey
items.description: Employment tops list of barriers for B.C. newcomers seeking homeownership
items._ogDesc: Employment tops list of barriers for B.C. newcomers seeking homeownership
items.body:
Most B.C. newcomers see owning a property as an important sign of establishment, but securing more stable or higher-paying employment is their biggest barrier to homeownership, according to a new survey.

About seven in 10 (71 per cent) B.C. newcomers who don’t own a home said they plan to buy one. Among them, two in five (40 per cent) said they plan to purchase within one to two years, according to the Royal LePage 2026 Canadian Newcomers survey released Thursday.

While renting is an option for many British Columbians who find the housing market unaffordable, newcomers have a strong intention to purchase their own home. About 90 per cent of B.C. newcomer respondents said homeownership is important or somewhat important to them, according to the survey.

“Homeownership has long been a defining goal for Canadians, and for newcomers it can carry added significance as they establish themselves in a new country and community,” said Phil Soper, president and CEO of Royal LePage, in a statement.

Despite homeownership being a priority, many newcomers have yet to enter the market. More than a quarter of (27 per cent) of B.C. newcomers are property owners, the lowest among Canadian provinces and below the 34 per cent national average.

Among B.C. newcomers who do not own a home, 86 per cent rent, according to the survey.

B.C. newcomers face a different set of barriers to homeownership than newcomers nationally. More than half (53 per cent) of B.C. respondents cited securing more stable or higher-paying employment as their biggest obstacle, followed by saving for a down payment (51 per cent). Nationally, the order was reversed.

“[Newcomers] face many of the same affordability challenges as Canadian-born buyers, from saving for a down payment to finding a property that meets their needs and budget,” said Soper.

“At the same time, they are likely learning an entirely new housing and financial system.”

About 26 per cent of B.C. newcomers said building their credit score or history in Canada has slowed their pace of purchasing a home, while 25 per cent said their source of income is unconventional or difficult to document, posing additional challenges for homeownership.

Where newcomers first settle also plays an important role in their homebuying decisions. Seven in 10 B.C. respondents said they still live in the same city or town where they first arrived in Canada, while 71 per cent of B.C. newcomer homeowners said they bought their home in the city or town where they first settled.

“Newcomers often put down roots where they already have a sense of culture, community and connection. Being close to family, familiar businesses and services in their mother tongue can play a significant role in where they choose to live,” said Raj Gill, a broker at Surrey-based Royal LePage Global Force Realty.

“Given affordability challenges in Metro Vancouver, many first-time buyers gravitate toward condominiums and townhomes rather than detached houses. Access to transit and less home maintenance can be more appealing than having additional square footage.”

The survey polled 1,400 newcomers, who immigrated to Canada within the past 10 years, between Aug. 25 and Sept. 8, 2026.

The post Most Canadian Households Now Run A Deficit To Meet Inflation: BoC appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: A new Bank of Canada report shows most households didn't beat inflation. Most households are now racking up debt to meet expenses.
items.body:
Canadian households may not acknowledge it publicly, but they’re falling behind. Bank of Canada (BoC) research shows incomes beat inflation from 2020 to 2025. But the researcher warns there’s a catch, as the average often cited by policymakers is an average. Most households didn’t beat inflation, and are now racking up debt every year to meet their expenses. The problem is amplified for those who are young, poor, or—wait, own a home?

Canadian Household Expenses Are Rising Faster Than Incomes

Household bills have climbed aggressively, but so has income—at least at the headline. From 2020 to 2025, the research found households spent $6,500 more on average. Over the same span, incomes grew an average of $7,400, leaving a $900 annual surplus. That’s not ideal, but at least it’s positive. Unfortunately, the average is hiding the budget pressures most households are facing.

The 2022 to 2024 inflationary shock led to a persistent erosion in buying power. Spending exceeded income, flipping the gap into negative territory. By 2025, inflation calmed and income surpassed spending again, but only by $274. “Spending growth did outpace income gains between 2022 and 2024 as elevated inflation pushed spending higher,” explains BoC senior researcher Yaz Terajima, the author of the report.

Inflation eased but that doesn’t change the narrowing of the gap already created. “Although a lower rate of inflation means consumer prices are rising more slowly than before, it does not erase the effects of higher prices that households have had to absorb since the pandemic began,” explains Terajima.

Averaging isn’t just hiding the pain over time. It’s also concealing that most households have negative cashflow.

Most of Canada’s Households Are Accumulating Debt Annually

Canada’s wealthier households skew the average, distorting the picture. Incomes failed to keep up with the cost of living for the bottom 60% of households, a.k.a. most. The 5th quintile, top 20%, had a healthy average surplus of $14,006 in 2025. However, the 20% below them saw an average of less than a quarter that amount, averaging just $3,047. It turns negative for the rest of the country, with the 3rd quintile facing a $4,811 annual shortfall. The shortfall for the 2nd quintile was the biggest at $6,805, while the 1st—or bottom 20%—saw a $4,236 shortfall. The reason for the smaller shortfall in the bottom 20% is likely explained by credit access. When you’re broke, you borrow money to pay the bills. When you’re truly poor, you just stop eating.

Age plays a role, surprising no one in Canada. “While many households saw income growth offset higher spending, others—particularly younger and lower-income households—did not,” explains Terajima.

When he separated the 2025 data by household age groups, those under 35 had an annual shortfall of $4,249. They were the only age group in negative territory, but the trend wasn’t as blunt as just an age-related issue. The narrowest surplus was ages 55 to 64, who had a surplus of only $169 annually. It’s a surplus, but barely. seniors 65+ had over 3x that amount at $618, while peak earners ages 45 to 54 had a $1,781 surplus—10x larger.

It’s easy to assume that housing related wealth plays a role here, but not in the way we initially suspected. Homeowners had an average annual shortfall of $1,817, while renters had an average of just $90 annually. Both are negative, but those with a home are spending a lot more than they make these days.

The homeowner data point may be hard to reconcile with the other data points at first. Annual shortfalls are concentrated in younger, less wealthy households… that own all the homes? That seems odd since being young and broke isn’t often associated with ownership in Canada. The BoC doesn’t address it in the report, but it’s a side effect of a real estate bubble.

Nearly half of homeowners are mortgage free, and those tend to be older households. We’ve discussed how the average mortgage payment is lower than rent, but not if you’re a recent buyer. Buyers at the frenzy’s peak 5-6 years ago are carrying much larger mortgages. The negative skew suggests this minority’s shortfall is so large that it puts the entire average in the red.

Financial experts are warning there’s a disturbing accumulation of debt in Canada. Households are using debt to “smooth” consumption, according to credit rating agency TransUnion. That’s a fancy way of saying inflation beats their income, and they’re borrowing to fill the hole with debt. It’s not just poor financial management.

RBC warned that most parents are subsidizing their adult children’s living expenses. A problem that remains stubbornly high even as those children approach middle age.

But the important thing is inflation is low and stable, according to the BoC’s council. Just ignore the 2021 measurement change that was expected to chronically underreport CPI. It’s a mystery how that worked out.

items.title: Definitions in Ottawa's budget framework are inconsistent: fiscal watchdog
items.description: Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog says the way the Liberal government defines certain types of spending in its new budget framework can be inconsistent.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan adjusts the microphone as she waits to appears before a committee in Ottawa on Monday, March 23, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog says the way the Liberal government defines certain types of spending in its new budget framework can be inconsistent.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog says the way the Liberal government defines certain types of spending in its new budget framework can be inconsistent and contradictory.

The Liberals under Prime Minister Mark Carney introduced a new budget framework that divides spending between day-to-day operating expenses and measures to stimulate capital investment.

A report released Thursday by the office of parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan attempts to track Ottawa’s path to balancing the operating side of the budget — a key fiscal anchor set by the Carney government.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The budget office says the government is improving fiscal transparency in some ways by offering explanations of how certain tax incentives, loan guarantees and other measures — the kind that normally would fall outside traditional accounting definitions of capital spending — are helping to meet its fiscal anchor.

But the PBO also argues the way Ottawa defines its operating and capital categories isn’t as stringent as the definition used in other jurisdictions that use a similar framework, such as the United Kingdom and Singapore.

For example, two programs under Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada appear contradictory in their accounting. The Agricultural Clean Technology and Agricultural Climate Solutions programs both encourage farms to invest in technology to reduce greenhouse gas emissions — but only the former program is considered capital spending under the framework.

The PBO says it found a broad pattern of spending programs like these that could arguably be classified as either operating or capital. The lack of “consistent, published rationale” on how to classify spending makes it hard to judge how future spending decisions will be sorted, the office says.

“Classification-based fiscal rules like the operating budget fiscal anchor do not limit overall government borrowing, and there is a risk that the classification definition can be arbitrary or change over time,” the report says.

Carney said last week the federal government is on track to balance its operating budget in fiscal 2027-28 — a year earlier than first promised.

The PBO projections anticipate Ottawa will instead hit that marker a year late, in fiscal 2029-30. Those estimates are based on federal figures as of the spring economic update in April, and do not include spending announcements or revenue changes over the summer.

John Fragos, spokesperson for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said Thursday the government is sticking by its pledge to balance the operating budget a year early.

“A persistent commitment to fiscal prudence, discipline, and spending efficiency — underpinned by the government’s $60 billion in savings — has moved up balancing the operating budget agenda by a whole year despite today’s report purporting otherwise,” he said in a statement.

He said a focus on reducing operating expenditures is a “stricter guardrail” for federal finances than ratios like debt-to-GDP. The federal government’s other fiscal anchor is maintaining a declining deficit-to-GDP ratio.

The PBO notes that in its projection stating the government will miss balancing the operating budget in 2028-29, the deficit posted in that fiscal year is relatively small.

But that only shows how the Liberals’ subjective definitions of capital and operating spending can influence the government’s ability to meet its fiscal targets, the PBO argues.

“Classifying even a modest amount of spending as capital rather than operating, without any actual change in fiscal policy, may have been relevant to balance the initial operating budget fiscal track,” the report says.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

items.title: Why exhaustion isn't proof of commitment, one leader says
items.description: A bank executive says women in mortgage wear burnout like a badge, and it needs to stop
items.content: <p>A bank executive says women in mortgage wear burnout like a badge, and it needs to stop</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639258745517757551.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A bank executive says women in mortgage wear burnout like a badge, and it needs to stop
items.body:
Exhaustion is not proof of commitment, and women in Canada's mortgage industry need to stop treating it as such, according to Janne Farias, chief internal auditor at Wealth One Bank of Canada.

Farias made the case on September 24, at the Women in Mortgage Summit Canada in Toronto, when the summit's leadership panel on burnout and boundaries was asked which habit women should let go of.

"I'd say is the fact if you are tired all the time doesn't mean that you're committed," Farias said.

"So we need to stop saying that, you know, if being exhausted or tired is a proof of commitment. So if you're always the person that people rely on, either your team or your management team, it doesn't mean that you're the most committed person in the room."

Read more: Mortgage rates aren't falling anytime soon, one economist warns

When capacity becomes the plan

"Build a system around you that is resilient, that you can actually delegate, that you can rely on other people," Farias said.

"Otherwise it becomes too much on us. And as women, we tend to do that. We always put our hands up for everything."

"Your team needs you at 100%. They don't need you at 100% access," she said. "How many times I've been in a meeting where I was there, but I was so exhausted."

Statistics Canada's 2022 Time Use Survey found women aged 15 and older spent an average of 3.7 hours a day on unpaid work, versus 2.6 hours for men.

At last year's summit keynote on mortgage burnout, Dr. Samra Zafar told attendees, "So don't wait for burnout before taking care of your mental health."

Leadership, learning, connection, and a lot of honest conversation. That's been the theme of the morning at the #WomenInMortgageCA Summit.

Stay tuned for more highlights!

Full Agenda: https://t.co/b04QQ6f7Bl pic.twitter.com/1zAyMENoxP — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) September 24, 2026

Why balance isn't perfection for mortgage leaders

Sofia Hondrogiannis, associate vice-president of national distribution, broker services, at TD Bank, and one of Canadian Mortgage Professional's Top 50 Women of Influence for 2026, offered a related lesson.

"I think I've learned that balance does not mean you have to be perfect at everything. Balance just means balance," she said.

"It's like, listen, it's not super all the time, and that's how it's gonna be, and you have to be okay with that."

Elena Robinson, vice-president of residential sales at First National Financial LP, described a similar shift.

"When I started, I worked damn hard, and I fixed things, and I was dependable. But now it's shifted," she said.

"I think that just letting go that you don't have to be that person anymore that does everything."

Read more: Why mentorship alone won't get more women into leadership

Moderator Leanne Conroy, regional director of sales at MCAN Home Mortgage Corporation, said that with "less mothering to do," she finds herself "taking on more because I have that time."

Farias, whose children are also older, said her husband now asks whether she is sure about volunteering for "one more thing."

"But then I said no yesterday," she said, "so which is a good thing."

items.title: The fine print that can turn a 6% private loan into 14%
items.description: One lender says he's seen payout statements that are "eye-watering"
items.content: <p>One lender says he's seen payout statements that are "eye-watering"</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639258724477379777.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: One lender says he's seen payout statements that are "eye-watering"
items.body:
A private mortgage priced at 5.99% with a 2% fee can balloon into a 14% loan if a broker misses an auto-renewal clause in the commitment, private lenders warned on September 24, the second day of MortgageFest Canada in Toronto.

Jason Geall, chief executive and principal broker at Peerage Mortgage Capital Inc. in Toronto, laid out the scenario during a Day Two panel on private and mortgage investment corporation (MIC) lending.

"What I've seen and hear a lot – it's unfortunate – is that some lenders have auto-renewal fees that can be really scary. You could have a really cheap upfront rate and fee, which sounds fantastic," Geall said.

"But then if they don't renew and it auto-renews, the rate goes up by 3.5%, there's a 4% auto-renewal fee, and all of a sudden your 5.99% and 2% is now 14%, and they're locked in. It's closed for 6 months or for a year, and they're handcuffed."

Read more: CMHC economist: the condo model itself may not survive

Why private mortgage costs don't stop at the rate

Nick Christopoulos, chief executive of Hosper Mortgage, said brokers routinely compare private lenders on the wrong numbers.

"A lot of brokers think it's just about interest rate and placement fee. And when you actually compare lenders, there's a big disparity in the schedule of fees – the fees that they charge for administration, for discharge, for enforcement actions," he said.

"On an annualized basis, these fees can be upwards of 3, 4, 5%."

Hosper has previously warned brokers about backend penalties and hidden fees in private deals.

Sebastien Kuperhause, vice-president of sales at Sequence Capital, said the exit deserves equal scrutiny.

"Understand it's not just the cost on the way in, it's the cost on the way out. What is the true cost to your client? Because what is it at renewal when you have to renew? And then what are the discharge fees? I've seen some payout statements and it was eye-watering – just absolutely eye-watering what they're being charged to get out."

Read more: Mortgage rates aren't falling anytime soon, one economist warns

What regulators expect brokers to document

Moderator Donna Thornton, a board member of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association – Ontario (CMBA-ON), said clients who get trapped are what bring the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) calling.

"We get phone calls from our friends at FSRA saying, 'Please show us why this was suitable, how you came to that,'" she said.

"From the regulator's perspective, it's not just enough to have your client sign the suitability and the exit strategy form. You need to take notes."

FSRA's suitability guidance says brokerage documentation should, at minimum, record the product recommendation and the reasoning for how it meets the client's needs and circumstances. In July, the regulator refused to renew an Ontario broker's licence over unsuitable private mortgages arranged for elderly clients.

Renewal offers no safety net either, said Joe Flor, vice-president of national sales and broker relations at CMI Canadian Mortgages Inc.

"When it comes to renewal in the private space, it's never a guarantee. It's a privilege," he said.
