items.title: Private mortgage awareness gap persists, report finds
items.description: Canadians who turn to alternative lenders report stronger financial outcomes, yet most still see private mortgages as a last resort
items.content: <p>Canadians who turn to alternative lenders report stronger financial outcomes, yet most still see private mortgages as a last resort</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639258564064429377.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canadians who turn to alternative lenders report stronger financial outcomes, yet most still see private mortgages as a last resort
items.body:
An awareness gap around private mortgage lending persists across Canada, even as those who have used alternative financing report overwhelmingly positive results, according to a new national study released this week.

The 2026 Canadian Private Mortgage Lending Report, commissioned by CMI Financial Group, one of Canada's largest non-bank lenders, and conducted by Angus Reid, finds that just six per cent of Canadians have used a private mortgage lender, but more than half of those borrowers (56 per cent) say the experience improved their long-term financial standing. Only 11 per cent reported a negative outcome.

The findings point to a perception problem that financial advisors and mortgage brokers may be uniquely positioned to address.

"Canadians' financial lives look very different today from how they were in decades past," said Bryan Jaskolka, CEO of CMI Financial Group, which has funded more than $4 billion in mortgages over more than 20 years in business. "The economics have largely changed, while the criteria for traditional mortgage financing have only become more stringent."

Widespread unfamiliarity shapes perception

Despite nearly two-thirds of Canadians (64 per cent) having at least heard of alternative mortgage lending, only six per cent describe themselves as very familiar with how it works. That limited understanding appears to be driving negative perceptions: 39 per cent of respondents called private mortgages a "last resort," while 37 per cent described them as "risky."

Only one in four Canadians (26 per cent) has either personally considered using a private lender or knows someone who has. Three-quarters have had no direct or indirect exposure at all. For advisors working with clients who are struggling to qualify through traditional channels, this knowledge gap represents both a challenge and an opportunity.

The role of brokers in closing that gap is already evident. Among Canadians who have considered alternative lending, more than half (52 per cent) say they first learned about it through a mortgage broker - underscoring how professional guidance shapes borrower confidence and decisions.

Who is actually turning to private mortgages

The most common reason Canadians sought out a private mortgage lender was to finance a first home or primary residence (71 per cent). Among those borrowers, 56 per cent considered alternative financing because it offered better rates or more flexible terms than major banks could provide.

Ontarians were the most likely to have used an alternative lender (nine per cent), while only 15 per cent of Quebecers reported using or considering a private mortgage.

Income also plays a significant role: Canadians earning more than $100,000 annually were more likely to consider alternative lending (45 per cent) and had the highest familiarity with the space (72 per cent), while those earning under $50,000 were least likely, with 38 per cent viewing it as risky.

Midlife Canadians between the ages of 35 and 54 showed the most openness, with more than one in three (37 per cent) saying they are familiar with alternative lending and 51 per cent indicating willingness to consider it if they could not access traditional financing.

Younger borrowers aged 18 to 34 showed a similar pattern: despite 37 per cent still viewing private mortgages as risky, 67 per cent of those who went ahead reported an improvement in their financial position, and 80 per cent cited better mortgage rates or terms as their primary motivation.

The gap between reputation and reality

Barriers to homeownership remain real for a significant share of Canadians.

While 67 per cent of respondents said they faced no obstacles in securing a mortgage, the remaining 33 per cent cited limited down payment savings (10 per cent), high property prices (eight per cent), self-employment or irregular income (seven per cent), mortgage stress test requirements (three per cent), and credit history (two per cent) as the most common hurdles.

Alternative lending which includes loans provided by private lenders or mortgage investment corporations (MICs) rather than banks or credit unions, is typically used as a short-term bridge toward conventional financing. It often comes with higher interest rates and fees, but places greater weight on property equity and the borrower's overall plan than on income documentation or credit score.

"Alternative lending can act as a bridge towards conventional financing while they stabilize their financial situation," Jaskolka said. "This doesn't mean it's the right solution for every borrower, but it shows that these solutions should be assessed based on someone's circumstances rather than reputation alone."

For brokers whose clients are increasingly gig workers, self-employed, or earning income outside traditional employment structures, the findings suggest that the private mortgage conversation may be overdue. Given that more than half of those who used alternative lending reported a positive long-term outcome, the data makes a case for brokers to become more fluent in the space, not to advocate for private mortgages by default, but to ensure clients aren't ruling them out based on reputation alone.

items.title: Mortgage rates aren't falling anytime soon, one economist warns
items.description: She says today's rate could be the best one your client sees for a while
items.content: <p>She says today's rate could be the best one your client sees for a while</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639258711189960022.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: She says today's rate could be the best one your client sees for a while
items.body:
Mortgage brokers counting on a Bank of Canada rate cut may need to reset client expectations, according to Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC), who sees higher borrowing costs over the next six to 12 months.

Speaking at the Women in Mortgage Summit Canada in Toronto on September 24, Cooper said a global selloff in US Treasuries, stubborn US inflation and Canada's tariff-driven price pressures leave the central bank little room to ease.

"So we'll be forced into raising interest rates. Not necessarily in October, but I think unfortunately probably by later this year or early the first half of next year," she said.

That is a sharper stance than she took in late August, when she expected the Bank of Canada to hold steady for the rest of the year.

Read more: MortgageFest Day 1 recap: Industry leaders on the path forward for brokers

Why bond markets are pushing mortgage rates higher

Cooper tied the shift to the US government's $40-trillion debt and to geopolitical instability. She said these have driven heavy selling of US Treasuries and pushed long-term yields sharply higher, a trend already feeding into Canadian fixed mortgage rates as the trade war escalates.

Canada's five-year bond yield, the benchmark for fixed-rate pricing, jumped 14 basis points in a single day this week, she said. "That's unheard of."

The US Federal Reserve lifted its benchmark rate 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% on September 16, its first hike since 2023. The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on September 2 for a seventh straight meeting, while Statistics Canada put August inflation at 3%.

Read more: A BoC rate hike soon? One top economist isn't buying it

Cooper said Canada's fiscal footing is far stronger than that of the US, but warned that retaliatory tariffs will push domestic prices higher. The big banks are split on whether the Bank of Canada will hike this fall, with National Bank and Scotiabank projecting a move to 2.50% in October.

Tanya Woods, managing director and head of government and regulatory affairs at Questrade, shared that view. "Ultimately, rates will probably rise, but they're trying to hold as long as possible," she said.

Day 2 of #MortgageFestCanada 2026 is underway! 🚀 Alongside another day of insightful sessions and networking, we're proud to host the #WomenInMortgageCA Summit, bringing together industry leaders for conversations on leadership, growth, and the future of mortgage lending. ✨ pic.twitter.com/FfUGamICZh — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) September 24, 2026

What should brokers tell clients now?

"So it is a time when we should encourage anyone that is interested in potentially buying a home that they get pre-approved, because today's rates, even though they're a little above what they were last week and the week before, they're only going higher," Cooper said.

Most of the brokers she has worked with over the past 15 years, she noted, have never seen a bond bear market.

She added that "we have to expect higher interest rates, which also means that fixed-rate mortgages are very attractive now."

The Bank of Canada's next rate announcement is October 28.

items.title: 7,500-Unit Master Plan On Former Military Air Field Breaks Ground In Prince Edward County
items.description:
Prince Edward County — land of wineries, farms, and quaint storefronts — will soon be home to one of Ontario’s largest residential developments: a 7,500-unit master-planned community located on the site of a WWII military air field. Dubbed Base31, the lands have undergone significant transformation since being purchased by developers in late 2021. But last Friday marked the biggest milestone yet, with the groundbreaking of the development’s first residential projects.

The 750-acre site is located two kilometres south of the rural town of Picton, roughly 160 km east of Toronto and just 14 minutes from the sloping dunes of Sandbanks Provincial Park. It’s a quiet place, but one with a rich history the developers are tapping into.

A rich history

In 1940, The Canadian Government built a 70-acre military training base on the site called No.31 Bombing and Gunnery School. It was operated by the British Royal Airforce, who trained young men that had travelled from the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand to become army airmen. After the war, the base served as a technical training and support hub for the Royal Canadian Air Force and Canadian Army until 1970, when it was bought by former Picton mayor H.J. McFarland and repurposed for light industrial use. But by the 2000s, the site’s barracks, mess halls, hangars, and administrative buildings had started being co-opted by local artisans and small businesses.

In 2021, PEC Community Partners Inc., purchased the site with the goal of leaning into this art- and community-focused revitalization of the former military lands, and began restoring the site’s aging concrete and cedar shake buildings. This led to the creation of B31 District — a central cultural hub hosting music concerts in the old drill hall, art exhibitions, and open-air food markets.

The master plan

B31 District serves as the heart of the forthcoming master-planned community, which will consist of residential villages, an extensive system of open space ‘green fingers,’ and natural areas, including 270 acres of protected green space and 10.5 km of trails. The development is projected to take around 20 to 25 years to complete, and will be carried out in several phases. On Friday, phase one broke ground with Hilltop Village, the first residential village at Base31, and The Landing, its first purpose-built rental building.

The Landing will provide 120 units, and Hilltop’s Village A will deliver 458 homes, including two-storey detached homes, bungalows, twin-entry townhomes, mews townhomes, and more starting at $299,900. “One concept that is embedded in the entire project is housing for all,” says Alexandra De Gasperis, Vice-President of DECO Communities, the principal development partner and community builder for Base 31. “So there is something for everyone at every stage of their life.”

In terms of design, the homes will reflect existing styles in the community. “The county has beautiful Victorian-era homes and farmhouses,” says De Gasperis. “We went around and took a significant amount of photos for inspiration, and Hunt Design reimagined it in a more modern form for us.”

Affordability is another key aspect of the development. In total, 5% of the roughly 7,500 homes will be affordable and, earlier this month, Base 31 and Habitat for Humanity Prince Edward-Hastings announced a partnership to deliver affordable townhouses within Hilltop. As well, 10% of The Landing units will be affordable, with rents expected to start around $1,000 per month for the affordable units and $1,450 per month for market rate studio units.

By providing a range of housing types at more attainable price points, De Gasperis says she hopes the development will attract a diverse community of future Pictonians. Two of the main groups she expects to move in are seniors who have sold their properties and city and want to retire in an amenity-rich community, young people priced out of city centres, and locals who grew up in the county but can’t afford PEC’s $700,000 average price point. Amenities planned for the community reflect that diverse customer base. Already available at the B31 District are amenities like public sports courts, a sensory garden for kids, a daycare, art galleries, and restaurants.

The first village is expected to be completed within 10 years, with the first phase finished in just over two years.

Big changes

Once occupied, the expansive development could more than quadruple the population of Picton, which currently sits around 4,500 people. Many are excited about the opportunities that growth would bring and the substantial addition to the region’s housing supply, but others have pushed back on the unprecedented development. According to the Toronto Star, some residents are concerned the development won’t deliver enough affordable housing and that it will ruin Picton’s small-town charm.

De Gasperis pushes back on this narrative. “This is a long-term plan. We're not in a rush to get there. We've consulted significantly with the community and we faced very little opposition throughout our entire planning process,” she says. “We don't want to change the context of this place. We don't want to change it from being this rural community. We're very mindful about doing this at a pace and in a way that is complimentary of the things that are already happening here.”

There’s also been significant concern that Picton will get stuck with a $255.5 million bill for new water and wastewater infrastructure needed to sustain the 7,500 additional homes. The worry is that if the market remains soft, development at Base31 could stall and the development charges needed to cover these infrastructure costs would remain unpaid, leaving the city millions in debt. But De Gasperis says those water infrastructure updates are unavoidable if Picton wants to see any future development, not just the realization of Base31.

“The water treatment plant in Picton is 99 years old, and it is reaching the end of its useful life. Then there is a water and wastewater treatment plant in Wellington that are at full capacity. You cannot flush a single additional toilet without building upon those facilities,” she says. “The county recognizes that the Provincial Policy Statement requires municipalities to have capacity for future development, but there's a significant quantum that is involved in that. [...] People in the county look at that number and think that is a really high number. But what I don’t think they recognize is that most of that number needs to be paid whether or not new housing comes on.”

In reality, Base31 will only owe a fraction of the $255.5 million sum, though De Gasperis says they don’t know what the exact number will be.

items.title: Small-Scale Infill Is (Finally) Showing Up In Toronto’s Housing Data
items.description:
Small-scale infill projects have gone from a barely noticeable share of Toronto’s housing starts to a more meaningful one in just two years, according to a new analysis from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC). Last year, smaller infill projects — accessory dwelling units and buildings with two to eight units — accounted for 6.45% of the city’s total housing starts, and while that figure may seem slight, it’s up more than tenfold from 0.62% in 2023.

The growth of small-scale infill has been particularly pronounced in a handful of other Canadian cities. In Vancouver, these projects accounted for 18.07% of total housing starts in 2025, up from 13.22% in 2023. Edmonton saw an even larger increase, from 9.95% to 23.28% over that two-year course. CMHC describes Calgary as also having ”strong growth in small-scale infill.”

“Uptake has been slower in Ontario overall, partly reflecting weaker housing starts in recent years,” the national housing agency says. “However, in places like Toronto, small-scale infill starts have still increased even during an overall slowdown.”

Small-scale infill share of housing starts in Toronto, Vancouver, and Edmonton/CMHC

In a separate analysis from last year, CMHC noted that residential-to-residential infill conversions have actually become the leading form of “missing middle” housing development in Toronto.

“Limited availability of undeveloped land makes gentle density through infill development a necessity,” said CMHC. “Notably, during the first half of 2025, there were over four times as many units initiated through conversion than there’ve been combined single- and semi-detached starts on new foundations. Unlike high-rise construction, which is concentrated in the downtown core, infill conversions are happening across the city.”

Recent zoning reforms have made these types of projects more common. In May 2023, Toronto City Council approved as-of-right permissions for multiplexes of up to four units — a move that paved the way for duplexes, triplexes, and fourplexes in areas where they were previously restricted. The city has continued to expand its multiplex permissions since, and today, as-of-right allowances for five and sixplexes have been extended to nine out of 25 wards.

Housing starts for one to eight unit developments/CMHC

The regional growth in small-scale infill is in line with a nation-wide shift in how new housing is being delivered. CMHC estimates that small-scale infill accounted for around 10% of Canada’s total housing starts last year. Single-detached housing starts have been falling since 2016, but the uptick in small-scale infill has managed to make up for at least some of the decline.

“Its share of total housing starts was falling until about 2023, before rising sharply to surpass 2016 levels,” says CMHC. “The timing of this reversal coincides with the launch of the Housing Accelerator Fund, as well as municipal and provincial reforms, such as Bill 23 in Ontario, and Bill 44 in British Columbia. Together, these changes allowed more small-scale infill housing to be developed on lots that historically contained a single home.”

Though the growth of small-scale infill is notable, the predominant form of infill is Canada has long been larger in scale. CMHC estimates that infill developments with nine units or more accounted for 63% of national housing starts last year, driving the share of total starts on previously developed land up to 60.17%. A decade earlier, those figures were 42% and 54.5%, respectively.

items.content: <p>Brokers highlight fast funding and hands-on underwriting support at Calvert Home Mortgage</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639216450115808372.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Brokers highlight fast funding and hands-on underwriting support at Calvert Home Mortgage
items.body:
For Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation, being named among Canadian Mortgage Professional’s Brokers on Lenders 2026 winners confirms something the company has worked at for decades: treating every interaction with its broker partners as a chance to make their jobs a little easier. Rather than positioning itself purely as a funding source, it has built its reputation on being the team standing behind every broker relationship, pairing underwriting expertise with responsive business development and operational support.

That reputation has been decades in the making. Calvert Home Mortgage was founded in 1975 by Everett Koeller as a family-owned mortgage lender headquartered in Calgary, Alberta and has since grown into an established Mortgage Investment Corporation (MIC).

A five-decade track record in exit-driven lending

The lender reports it has funded more than 12,000 deals and loaned in excess of $2.9 billion, supporting over 11,000 real estate investors, mortgage brokers, and homeowners across Alberta and Ontario.

Calvert Home Mortgage points to five core values as the foundation of that growth, namely service, trust, education, people, and solutions. That philosophy starts with trust. “Our philosophy is simple: be available, honest, and solutions-oriented,” says Ryan Day, Head of Business Development at Calvert Home Mortgage. “That’s how you earn a broker’s trust, and that’s how their clients end up having a great experience.”

For Day, the stakes go beyond a single transaction. “A mortgage broker’s reputation is built one client experience at a time,” he says. “We see our role as making sure every one of those experiences is seamless so brokers can consistently deliver the kind of outcomes that keep clients coming back.”

That focus on speed shows up in how Calvert Home Mortgage structures its lending. The firm advertises funding turnaround as fast as one to two business days in Alberta and one to three business days in Ontario once all required documents are received, a pace built specifically around the time-sensitive nature of the deals brokers bring to the table. Its product range, spanning flip financing, bridge loans, equity take-out, debt consolidation, and transitional closed-term mortgages, is designed to give brokers flexibility when a client’s circumstances do not fit a standard lending model.

What Calvert Home Mortgage’s underwriting team brings to the table

On the underwriting side, Garrett LaBarre, Underwriter Manager, frames the relationship in similar terms. “I believe mortgage brokers value our underwriting support because we don’t approach their files as paperwork,” LaBarre says. “Behind each deal is a client counting on their broker, and we take that responsibility very seriously. To me, this result reflects that mortgage brokers see us as true partners in the process, working alongside them to achieve the best outcome rather than just processing the submissions.”

That approach, he adds, depends on listening as much as processing. “Brokers have a deep understanding of their clients, and our role is to ensure that insight is fully reflected throughout the underwriting process. Success comes from genuinely listening to the context and expertise they bring to each file, rather than simply working through a checklist. When we do that well, we can make more informed decisions and deliver better outcomes for everyone involved.”

Calvert Home Mortgage’s Net Promoter Score sits at 85 percent as of fall 2025, drawn from its broker and real estate investor client base. Its annual customer feedback survey points to four consistent themes behind why brokers choose the lender.

Why brokers choose Calvert Home Mortgage

  • Speed and responsiveness: rapid file review, quick turnarounds, and dependable communication
  • Ease of doing business: common-sense underwriting, clarity of process, and the ability to speak with decision-makers
  • People and partnership: consistent praise for knowledgeable, collaborative underwriters who help solve problems rather than create friction
  • Product fit: Flexible mortgage solutions for real estate investment opportunities and borrowers on the path to traditional financing

For LaBarre, the significance lies less in any single strength and more in its consistency. “What stands out to me is not any single category, but the consistency of broker feedback across turnaround time, underwriter support, service levels, business development support, and transparency,” he says.

“That level of consistency suggests this isn’t the result of one team performing well; it reflects a coordinated effort across the entire organization. When mortgage brokers bring us a complex file, they’re not just looking for a quick response; they’re looking for a partner who will take the time to understand the client’s unique circumstances, collaborate on solutions, and find a way to make the deal work.”

That coordination, both spokespeople suggest, is what brokers are really looking for when a complex file lands on their desk, not just a fast answer but a partner willing to work through a client’s circumstances alongside them. For Calvert Home Mortgage, this year’s recognition reinforces a standard the lender intends to keep building on, one file and one broker relationship at a time.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s shrinking population was revised to show growth the whole time, eliminating the explanation for slow economic growth.
items.body:
And just like that, Canada’s shrinking population went the way of its technical recession—revised away. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows that the country’s population grew in Q3 2026. More importantly, the data includes the upward revisions we’ve been discussing for months. It turns out that the much-discussed population contraction plaguing the country didn’t exist. The revisions reveal a bigger population, but more importantly, a much worse economy.

Canada’s “Shrinking” Population Has Been Growing This Whole Time

Canadian quarterly population estimates: Reported vs latest revisions.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canada’s population climbed 0.2% (+80.3k people) to 41.8 million in Q3 2026, rising 0.5% (+189.4k) since last year. Annual growth is the weakest since Q2 2021, roughly the end of the pandemic’s lockdowns. The strength is likely to surprise most people, as the country was supposed to be shrinking. Our first hint that this wasn’t true should have been policymakers promising to do just that.

Canada’s Temporary Resident Estimates: Under On Decline, Inflated At Peak

StatCan made sharp revisions to its population estimates, as we previously warned. They originally reported a 0.5% y/y drop for Q2 2026, marking a rare annual decline. This morning’s update shows they missed roughly 300,000 people. Whoops!

The entire revision is due to methodology changes for estimating non-permanent residents (NPRs). There were 2.78 million NPRs in Q3 2026, down 0.7% (-18.9k) from last quarter and 5.3% (-154.6k) below last year’s estimates. However, Q2 2026 also saw an upward revision of 2.8 million, 9.3% (+239k people) higher than originally reported. The NPR peak in Q4 2024 was also revised lower from 3.15 million to 2.98 million, 5.4% (-170k) lower than reported. In short, even when policymakers launch half-baked plans, the numbers show stability. Cute.

Since these residents are in the country, it doesn’t change reality for consumption. Even if a bureaucrat forgets to count them, they still consume food and shelter. Demand-side pressures are the same. Policymakers may be delighted, as more human capital stock means higher credit capacity, however, reality doesn’t change, but the country’s economic narrative will.

Canada’s Upward Revisions Reveal A Much Worse Economy

Canada’s economy was doing really well for a country with a shrinking population. Now that it’s not shrinking, the economic reality is a disaster, validating how many feel. GDP growing 0.8% in Q2 2026 at the seasonally adjusted annual rate is impressive with a 0.5% population drop. Not so much if the population is growing 0.5% over that same period.

Breaking down that growth reveals how problematic those GDP numbers really were. Exports of goods represented 1.23 percentage points of that 0.8% growth, due mostly to higher oil prices. That means Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz did more for Canada’s GDP than its policymakers. A war between two other countries was a bigger boost than near-pandemic levels of new debt. The math is even more disturbing when it comes to the job market.

Canada’s employment data relies heavily on population estimates. The job data would have collected the number of NPRs with a job, but the population estimates wouldn’t have. This inflates the number of workers while underestimating the total number of people. We previously estimated that the undercount means the 6.7% unemployment rate is closer to 7.6%. That would make it the third-highest report since the pandemic, and it was a conservative call. We used the national average for the share in the labour force, but it’s typically much higher for NPRs.

StatCan confirmed it will revise the employment data in the coming months. However, the methodology means the revisions will be slowly introduced. Funny how reality can’t hit all at once when it impacts national optics negatively, eh?

The population revisions are surprising for a few reasons, and not just the upward ones. Upward revisions reveal a fragile economy, masked by ignoring hundreds of thousands of workers. They also make slow home sales and a sharp climb in rental vacancies even more troubling.

Downward revisions at the peak reveal the demand-side narrative was softer than presented. But what’s really surprising here is that they appeared at all. Our previous estimate shows StatCan overestimated the population for ~30 years. An agency study followed and found the overcount was even larger than our estimate. It appears revisions that expand the country’s borrowing capacity make it into official data faster than those that can slow it.

items.title: MortgageFest Day 1 recap: Industry leaders on the path forward for brokers
items.description: Top brokers have their say on the current market, how the profession must evolve, and much more
items.content: <p>Top brokers have their say on the current market, how the profession must evolve, and much more</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639258073076512943.jpeg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Top brokers have their say on the current market, how the profession must evolve, and much more
items.body:
Four of Canada’s top mortgage professionals took the stage at Day 1 of MortgageFest Canada to deliver an unfiltered assessment of where the market is headed – and how mortgage brokers can stay relevant and keep ahead in an increasingly hostile environment.

Prominent brokers Ron Butler (pictured top, middle left) of Butler Mortgage, Tracy Valko (pictured top, middle right) of DLC AMI Mortgage Collective Group, Vince Gaetano (pictured top, far right) of OwlMortgage.ca,  and moderator Frances Hinojosa (pictured top, far left) of Tribe Financial pulled no punches in a closing panel discussion that touched on rising bond yields, aggressive bank renewal tactics, and – colourfully – the limits of artificial intelligence.

The rate environment has grabbed headlines in recent weeks, with bond yields moving higher in a stark indication that fixed rates are also on the way up. Butler, who sees more Bank of Canada rate hikes on the horizon before the end of the year, said the pattern that follows any rate increase is a “valley of death”: an initial flurry of clients rushing to rate holds followed by a halt in activity as higher borrowing costs sink in.

As for home prices? He sees values continuing to fall before stabilizing at some point late next year. “When prices stop falling, they don’t immediately start going up. They stay flat for a while,” he said. “They just bounce around a little bit.”

Bond market trends and why brokers should follow them

South of the border, the Federal Reserve recently hiked interest rates, with that decision directly impacting Canadian fixed-rate pricing. Valko said understanding how bond market fluctuations affect the mortgage and housing outlook is simply not optional for brokers.

“You need to have that as the number one essential thing when you’re talking to your clients and your referral partners,” she said, “because it’s the only thing that’s going to help you navigate solutions for clients right now. And we know that narrative is continuously changing by the hour.”

Unsurprisingly, artificial intelligence (AI) also emerged as a prominent talking point, but Butler doesn’t see it having a dramatic impact on the industry in the years ahead – to put it mildly. “F*** AI… Forget it. It’s not going to change the mortgage business,” he said.

But Gaetano said the role of a mortgage broker still needs to evolve amid a constantly shifting economic backdrop. “We’ve got to go from being a gas station attendant to being a doctor,” he said.

“It’s no longer driving up, asking whether you want leaded or unleaded, and give them a five-year rate and see them in five years. You’ve got to evaluate what the client’s going through, what they’ve experienced, and what their household’s like.”

A troubling trend he’s seeing play out in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA): some clients who have owned their homes for 10 or 15 years now owe more today than they paid for them, not because of major renovations but because of lifestyle creep.

With property values declining and prime lending increasingly difficult to access, many are moving from prime into alternative and private solutions.

Value of mortgage brokers remains undimmed

The uber-attentive approach of banks to renewals was also a prominent topic of discussion. Some banking giants are aggressively early-renewing clients six to nine months out, often before brokers even know a renewal is approaching.

But an increasingly fraught outlook for mortgage borrowers and homeowners is also putting the value of brokers into clear focus, according to Valko. “One out of two Canadians are $200 away from not meeting their financial obligations,” she said.

“The numbers are there. You guys just need to pick up the phone and call the client. It’s not AI – it’s actually having calls.”

Another way for brokers to ride out the current storm and set themselves up for success in the current market cycle, according to Butler, is identifying a niche. “You have to have a specialty,” he said. “If you’re going to be an infinite generalist, you’re doomed.”

Plenty more is in store for Day 2 – be sure to attend what’s already been one of the biggest events in the Canadian mortgage industry calendar this year.

items.title: Why mentorship alone won't get more women into leadership
items.description: One executive says there's a second step most companies skip
items.content: <p>One executive says there's a second step most companies skip</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639257887412555237.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: One executive says there's a second step most companies skip
items.body:
Mentorship gives women in Canadian mortgage finance advice. Sponsorship gets them promoted. Senior lender executives say the industry still leans too heavily on the first.

That was the message from a women-in-leadership panel at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto today. Executives from First National Financial, Equitable Bank and MCAN Financial argued that leaders must actively open doors for women rather than simply counsel them. The session, moderated by Michele Steko, vice-president of national broker relations at Sherwood Mortgage Group, was part of a two-day programme that drew brokers and lenders to the International Centre.

"I think mentorship is for advice, but sponsorship is for opportunities," said Elena Robinson, vice-president of residential sales at First National.

"So you can mentor someone and give them that advice, but I think as leaders, we also have to sponsor, see the opportunity, see people that you think you could help them with their careers. And that's where the sponsorship piece comes in."

Why sponsorship matters for women in mortgage leadership

Zamina Walji, vice-president of growth businesses at Equitable Bank, described sponsorship as a leadership obligation.

Mentorship, she said, "is like advice. It's helping people navigate, but sponsorship is giving them that seat at the table. And like, as a leader, for me, that is my duty. It's not just to sponsor women, but it's to sponsor diversity so that you have diverse teams, diverse thought. And the way that you do that is by giving women high-impact roles, making them visible, making sure that they're presenting their work, that their voices are heard."

Robinson recalled spotting an underwriter she believed would excel in sales, a move that paid off.

"I think it's part of our responsibility is to watch and go out there and provide those opportunities so those individuals can grow in their careers," she said.

The panel's view matches findings in Canadian Mortgage Professional's Top 50 Women of Influence 2026 report. Judges there found mentorship language outnumbered sponsorship roughly two to one in nominations, yet the highest-scoring submissions showed sponsorship in action.

"Mentorship gives people advice, sponsorship gives them access," Paula Oliveira, regional vice-president for Ontario and Atlantic at BMO BrokerEdge, told CMP for that report.

There's plenty happening beyond the presentations at #MortgageFest Canada 2026! From interactive booth experiences and fun activations to valuable conversations with industry leaders, our sponsor and exhibitor hall is packed with opportunities to explore, engage, and connect! pic.twitter.com/7o0C0o53YN — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) September 23, 2026

How long will C-suite gender parity take?

The stakes are measured in generations. Leanne Conroy, regional director of sales at MCAN Financial, cited an estimate of about 100 years before men and women reach parity in the C-suite.

"I'll be dead unless I cryogenically freeze myself, but that's just a really long time," she said.

Broader data offer little comfort. The World Economic Forum's Global Gender Gap Report 2026 estimates full global gender parity is 120 years away at the current pace.

Participants in CMP's 2026 roundtable on women reshaping Canadian mortgage finance put women's share of CEO roles in the sector at 4%.

Conroy urged women to build trusted relationships beyond their own firms. "Those are the people who can work as your champion or as your sponsor that you know it's not in it for them," she said.

items.title: AI is making mortgage fraud nearly impossible to spot by eye
items.description: A MortgageFest Canada panel warns the fake ID on your desk may look entirely real
items.content: <p>A MortgageFest Canada panel warns the fake ID on your desk may look entirely real</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639257834365872210.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A MortgageFest Canada panel warns the fake ID on your desk may look entirely real
items.body:
Artificial intelligence is producing fake identification and forged mortgage documents that brokers can no longer reliably catch with a visual check. That was the warning from a TransUnion executive at MortgageFest Canada today.

Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, told a compliance panel that the money moving through Canadian real estate has made the sector a prime target for organized crime.

"Organized crime, there's way too much money to be made in the real estate industry ... it's going to get worse. I'm telling you right now, AI is making things a lot worse," Kuyper said.

"There's fake IDs out there. If you go to the Treefort booth, they will blow your mind with the fake IDs that they're showing there. Your eyes would not be able to distinguish that this is a fake ID."

Frances Hinojosa, CEO and co-founder of Tribe Financial Group, moderated the session. It was one of several compliance sessions on the MortgageFest Canada agenda.

The morning sessions at #MortgageFest Canada 2026 delivered practical insights on market trends, lending strategies, technology, and compliance!

Stay tuned for more highlights throughout the day!

View full agenda: https://t.co/PtUONuSEtO pic.twitter.com/5tIQmZtzYy — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) September 23, 2026

Why AI-forged mortgage documents slip past brokers

David Carter, a partner at law firm Grechi Carter, said lawyers do a fairly good job vetting identity fraud, backed by title insurers and verification software. The weaker link is income and appraisal paperwork.

"I think on the agent side, people are very much underestimating how much AI is helping fraudsters in putting together very credible and accurate-looking documents, whether it's on the income verification side or appraisal side, and using AI as a tool to help them perpetrate these frauds," Carter said.

Credit bureau data point the same way. Equifax Canada reported in April that first-party fraud, where applicants misrepresent their own finances, rose 31% nationally year over year in the fourth quarter of 2025, even as mortgage application fraud fell 12.5%.

Read more: AI is a gamechanger for mortgages – and brokers need to get on board

How simple questions can stop mortgage fraud early

"There are pretty significant ties between mortgage fraud and organized crime. So there's a lot of money behind this. They're very sophisticated, but they also don't want to get caught," Carter said.

"We find that often asking basic, simple questions at the outset will often scare off fraudsters. They don't want to be trying to get way down the road in a deal where they're going to get caught or where it's going to come to light."

Krista Zingel, senior director of compliance and broker development at Capital Mortgages, said brokerages must match lenders' investigative muscle.

"I'm not a cop, but I've had to beef up my investigation methodology for sure. I'll tell you, lenders, they have great investigations departments in-house, right? So we have to match that as well," Zingel said.

MortgageFest Canada runs across two full days, with Women in Mortgage Summit Canada scheduled for tomorrow, Sept. 24. The two events share the International Centre venue but operate independently, giving attendees the option to attend both.

items.title: Is AI eroding critical thinking in the workplace?
items.description: ‘Fluency without judgment simply helps an organization make mistakes faster’
items.content: <p>‘Fluency without judgment simply helps an organization make mistakes faster’</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0363_639256764975104030.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: ‘Fluency without judgment simply helps an organization make mistakes faster’
items.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is quietly wearing down the skill executives say matters most: critical thinking, according to an IBM report.

The research surveyed 1,500 chief human resources officers (CHROs) alongside 8,800 employees worldwide.

According to the study, 71% of CHROs identify the ability to supervise, validate and override AI outputs as the workforce's most essential skill, yet only 38% of employees agree. Sixty per cent of employees said AI is eroding their skills, and critical thinking was the capability most often cited as declining.

Geneviève Bich, Vice President - Human Resources (CHRO) at METRO, based in Düsseldorf, Germany, and a board member, framed the stakes for HR broadly: "AI is about enterprise transformation. It's about future of work. It's about competencies. It's about leadership. It's much more about all of this than about technology."

The erosion problem HR can't ignore

Enterprises are not ignoring the skills problem outright: 80% have a reskilling roadmap in place. But a roadmap addresses skill gaps, meaning the new competencies people need to use AI tools. Skill erosion is different: it describes capabilities employees already have quietly fading as AI absorbs more of the thinking work that once built them.

Nearly half of organizations – 46% – do not involve the CHRO when AI strategy is defined, the study found. Employee confidence in AI-enabled decisions rose in 63% of organizations where CHROs shared responsibility for defining which decisions stay human-led, compared with just 19% where they did not.

Statistics Canada's (StatCan) most recent data shows the share of Canadian businesses reporting AI use in producing goods or delivering services reached 19.2% in the second quarter of 2026, up from 6.1% two years earlier – nearly tripling. Data analytics was the most common application, at 36.6%, while 40.0% of businesses said AI was simply not relevant to their operations.

Why is judgment becoming HR's job to protect?

Dr. Amit Das, Director and Chief Human Resources Officer at Bennett Coleman & Co. Ltd. based in India, put the stakes bluntly: "Fluency without judgment simply helps an organization make mistakes faster," according to The Times of India. He also warned that "the real risk is the quiet erosion of the experiences through which people learn to think."

Only 23% of organizations are increasing entry-level hiring, while executives named experienced individual contributors and first-line managers – not early-career staff – as their priority investment. Some Canadian HR teams have started reworking how supervised exception handling gets built back into junior roles, a shift addressed in this overview of common pitfalls HR leaders face when deploying AI.

Nickle LaMoreaux, Senior Vice President and Chief Human Resources Officer at IBM Corporation, based in Armonk, New York, framed the moment as a turning point: "AI is changing not only how work gets done, but where people can contribute the greatest value. CHROs have a critical role to play in redesigning the workplace of the future so people can focus on the areas where they can have the greatest impact."

What does this mean for Canadian HR practice?

Many Canadian organizations are still building foundational AI governance rather than addressing skill erosion. Employers navigating fragmented rollouts across recruitment, benefits and performance tracking are documenting their approach, as captured in this monthly roundup tracking how AI adoption is reshaping Canadian HR functions.

StatCan found that among Canadian businesses using AI, 44.4% made changes to training or staffing practices as a result, with larger firms far more likely to retrain existing employees than smaller ones. The IBM report's recommendation for CHROs is similar: treat skill erosion as a talent risk on par with attrition, identifying which roles are losing exposure to analysis or exception handling, then rebuilding it through rotations and coaching.

A compensation dimension is emerging too. As demand grows for employees who can supervise and validate AI output, some Canadian employers are already paying a premium for that capability.

items.title: Canadian Renters Caught Between Higher Rents And Homes That Don't Fit
items.description:
Canadian renters with aspirations to move are facing much more than a logistical hassle, according to a new report on housing affordability from Statistics Canada (StatCan). The research, which draws from the fourth cycle of the Canadian Housing Survey, shows that moving in today’s private rental market comes at a premium, costing tenants hundreds of dollars more per month.

According to StatCan, the average monthly rent for tenants who had moved in the two years leading up to 2024 was $1,740, compared to $1,290 for sitting tenants who occupied their residence for at least two years. That translates to an average of $450 more per month — or $5,400 more per year — for renters who have recently moved.

And the nuances between sitting and mover tenants don’t end there. The national agency says that 40% of recent movers lived in unaffordable housing as of 2024, with 30% or more of pre-tax household income being spent on rent. That same metric for sitting tenants came in at 32%.

“Recent movers were also more likely to report financial difficulty due to increased rents (44.5%) and dissatisfaction with the affordability of their housing (45.5%) than their renter counterparts who had not moved recently (33.5% and 24.4%, respectively),” the report says.

“Since 2018, the share reporting financial difficulty due to rent increases rose by 27.0 percentage points for recent movers and by 16.5 percentage points for sitting tenants, which led to a widening of the gap between the two groups in recent years.”

StatCan’s findings point to a rental market reality where staying put comes with a significant financial advantage — one that many Canadians can’t afford to ignore, with more than one in ten living in core housing need: that is, housing that's unaffordable, doesn’t have enough bedrooms, or needs major repairs, while living somewhere else in the community is not affordable. At the same time, however, many renters are living in homes that no longer work for them.

According to a separate analysis of the Canadian Housing Survey from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), renters are currently living in dwellings with an average of 1.9 bedrooms, but aspire to have 2.6. That's a difference of around 37%.

Unsurprisingly, the gap is even more pronounced among renters living in “unsuitable housing” — defined by CMHC as a home that does not have enough bedrooms for the size and make-up of the household. Those households currently have an average of 1.8 bedrooms but aspire to have 3.3, marking an 84% difference.

CMHC says this gap illustrates “how far existing housing falls short of meeting their bedroom needs” and speaks to the “rise of overcrowded housing in Canada, especially in high-rent markets like Toronto and Vancouver.”

items.title: B.C. developers proceed cautiously as rental market softens
items.description: Slowing home construction could create future housing supply shortages in the province, experts warn
items._ogDesc: Slowing home construction could create future housing supply shortages in the province, experts warn
items.body:
B.C. developers are moving ahead with planned rental projects cautiously as softer demand and a growing supply of completed units put pressure on rents.

Asking rents in B.C. have fallen about 10 per cent over the past three years, the largest decline among Canadian provinces, according to Rentals.ca’s August report.

The decline comes as rental demand has weakened amid federal policies restricting international students and temporary workers, while a pipeline of new rental units continues to come onto the market, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. (CMHC).

But developers and economists warn that today's softer market could sow the seeds of a future supply shortage as construction activity slows.

“It is a very challenging real estate market, probably the hardest that many people have seen in their career that work in real estate,” said Josh Anderson, vice-president of development at Vancouver-based wealth management firm Nicola Wealth.

“We're taking a very conservative and measured approach to our development of multifamily housing in Vancouver.”

Nicola Wealth’s proposed rental project at 2111 Main St., a two-building development in Mount Pleasant, has received permits. The company said it hopes to start construction next year, with completion of the first building expected in 2030.

“When there's less demand, it's a lot harder for developers like ourselves or others to move forward,” said Anderson, adding that capital groups are much more reluctant to invest when they don’t see a strong immigration growth.

“And then you add how challenging the financing market is as well for construction financing. It definitely makes it a lot more difficult in today's market to move forward.”

However, Anderson said real estate development is a long-term investment that takes years to complete. Although it is not fully known when the market will recover, many in the industry believe there could be a change in the supply-and-demand curve towards the end of the decade, given how few projects are starting today.

New condo construction in Metro Vancouver hit a 15-year low in the first half of 2026, according to CMHC. Rental apartments accounted for most new constructions, supported by rental-focused policies and financing, while residential developments are struggling to secure financing through pre-sales, according to the organization.

“So that's why we see an opportunity towards the end of the decade to bring a project to market at that time,” said Anderson.

Others in the B.C. real estate industry have also felt the impact of more cautious decision-making toward condo development.

Jack Hui, managing principal of Pontem Group, a Vancouver-based building engineering and consulting firm, said some rental projects are moving forward, including some of his clients’ projects, but at a slower pace and with tighter budgets.

“In particular, those bigger developers, they don't want to lose the land, they don't want to lay off people, then the way that they actually create the portfolio is to create a rental [project],” said Hui.

But the way they do business has changed, he said, noting that competition is increasing for businesses such as his, and firms can easily be replaced if they don't perform or are not attuned to a project.

“The money is extremely tight. … We still have a lot of projects. It's just the average price has to be lower,” said Hui.

“On [the developers’] end, when they design and construct the building, they have to lower their cost as well. Otherwise, the pro forma is not going to work.”

Construction slowdown raises future supply concerns

Although softer rents are improving affordability for renters in the short term, weak construction activity could create supply constraints and put upward pressure on housing costs in the longer term, some experts said.

The number of rental condos in Metro Vancouver has continued to increase in recent years, rising 14 per cent from 93,961 in 2023 to 107,192 in 2025, according to CMHC.

At the same time, rental demand has softened amid fewer international students and temporary workers, and slower immigration growth.

“We still have quite a lot of number of units that are under construction that are becoming available in the next year or two,” said Shiva Moshtari Doust, lead economist for B.C. at CMHC.

“That's why we expect to see … the softer rental market environment continue unless there are changes with respect to the demand side of things.”

Metro Vancouver remains Canada’s priciest rental market despite falling rents, according to Rentals.ca. And Vancouver’s current pace of starts is still 5,000 to 7,000 units below what’s needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability levels by 2036, according to CMHC.

“Housing is not an overnight solution—it takes time,” Doust said.

“When demand comes back to the market, we want to make sure that there is supply to meet the need of that demand.”

This is echoed by Brendon Ogmundson, chief economist at the B.C. Real Estate Association, who warned that a slowdown in new home construction could eventually create a supply shortage, particularly if the pace of construction falls below the number of units needed.

“The real worry is that two or three years from now, because we haven't been building as many units as we need, we find ourselves at the end of this decade with a supply shortage,” he said.

He said this could become an issue as the province starts to see more international students and temporary foreign workers in the next few years, although those numbers are not expected to return to the levels seen in the early post-pandemic period.

“There's going to be a lot of interesting dynamics in the next couple of years,” he said.

items.description:
Remember when experts blamed Millennial home buying woes on avocado toast? Well, in Canada, Millennials now need help buying regular toast. Ditto with Gen Z, according to a new RBC survey. The post Most Canadian Parents Now Subsidize Their Adult Children’s Basic Living Costs: RBC appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: A new survey from RBC shows that most parents with adult children (ages 18 to 40) are helping with bills—primarily groceries and rent.
items.body:
Remember when experts blamed Millennial home buying woes on avocado toast? Well, in Canada, Millennials now need help buying regular toast. Ditto with Gen Z, according to a new RBC survey. The bank found that most parents are providing some form of financial help to their adult children between the ages of 18 and 40. However, the help isn’t for a down payment on a new home, but for groceries, rent, and utilities—assistance that remains disturbingly high even as these young adults approach middle age.

Canada’s Cost of Living Failure: Most Parents Need to Help Adult Children with Bills

Most parents (51%) need to help their adult children (ages 18 to 40) with bills, according to the survey. This is no longer just helping with a down payment to buy a home, but the collapse of stability for multiple generations. Nearly 1 in 3 (32%) of parents warn their children aren’t financially independent, while 35% of those providing support explicitly state the cost of living is too high for their adult children to stay afloat.

The younger these adults, the higher the odds of needing help. The survey found that more than 2 in 3 (68%) of parents are providing help for their 18-24-year-old adult children. Even among older cohorts (ages 35-40), the share of parents providing help was stubbornly high at 37%, almost 2 in 5.

Most Parental Help For Canada’s Young Adults Is For Groceries

The parental help isn’t for down payments, but many are forking over down payment amounts of cash. Over the past 12 months, parents provided an average of $6,151 in financial support for their adult children. Nearly 1 in 5 (18%) parents who provide support are giving between $10,000 and $19,999 annually. Inflation may be “low” according to StatCan, but the segments greatly outpacing CPI are the ones siphoning this cash—groceries, rent, and utilities.

Most of the parents providing support are paying for groceries (56%). The problem only slightly improved with age, with 43% of those with adult children aged 35-40 still helping with groceries. Help with groceries even outpaces unexpected emergencies (43%), which transforms this from a hiccup in finances to a systemic failure.

A quarter (24%) of parents providing financial help are helping with rents, a problem that worsens with age. Yes, you read that right. The share helping 18-to-24-year-olds matches the 24% average for all age brackets, but that climbs to 30% for those with children 30 to 34 years old.

Soaring energy bills and consumer debt are also contributing pressure. Utilities (21%) were the third-highest reason for help, followed by help paying off consumer debt (12%). The bank didn’t provide a breakdown, but TransUnion previously noted that consumer debt is increasingly being used to make ends meet, suggesting the accumulation may be an attempt to smooth the other three expenses that young adults are struggling to contain.

Canada’s Cost of Living Crisis Is A Structural Threat

Canada’s cost of living crisis is now a structural threat, dismissing the narrative that young adults are just making bad financial decisions. Only 15% of parents providing support cited poor money management as the reason for their help. The path to financial stability has structurally collapsed.

The wage-to-inflation mismatch has extended dependency into what should have been peak earning years, with 1 in 5 (19%) 35-to-40-year-olds still lacking financial independence. “This generation isn’t failing to launch. The runway has gotten longer and a lot more expensive,” says Melissa Leong, a personal finance expert cited in the bank’s report.

The fact that young adults need help in the current environment isn’t the only problem either. Parents also need to be vigilant, as their retirement incomes face the same hurdles in trying to beat the cost of living, regardless of what level CPI is reported.

“Put on your own financial oxygen mask first. As a parent, protect essential expenses, emergency savings, high-interest debt repayment and retirement before deciding what you can sustainably give,” warns Leong.

The bank’s report didn’t include a regional breakdown, but the most recent CPI report indicated this mismatch may skew by region—and not where many anticipate. CPI is currently hot nationally, but Eastern Canada is facing a much stronger inflationary environment. The problem is approaching crisis levels in provinces like Nova Scotia, where annual growth is now more than double the Bank of Canada’s target rate.

If you’re into golfing and have $45 million on hand, you can buy yourself a course.

Located on 48th Avenue in the City of Langley, the Newlands Golf & Country Club is back on the market, listed as a just over 111-acre club with more than 90,000-square-feet of improvements.

The listing notes those improvements include an 18-hole championship course and 11-hole executive course, banquet and wedding facilities for up to 700 people, the Newlands Care Centre and Montessori School, a bar and grill restaurant with a dining room, as well as several single-family homes.

The listing also notes the city’s current zoning for the site is P2, A1, RU-10, SR1.

The Official Community Plan (OCP) designation is mostly Institutional, intended to accommodate a variety of recreational and civic uses.

While the site is mostly within the Agricultural Land Reserve (ALR), the listing notes there is around two acres of development potential of near-to-medium term developable non-ALR land, as well as around four acres of long-term developable non-ALR land.

The listing also points out that the city’s OCP designation of Ground Oriented Residential allows for townhomes, rowhomes and multi-unit residential.

Meanwhile, in the City of Delta, the Delta Golf & Country Club which had been placed in a court ordered sale, is reopened after the owner secured refinancing.

The site earlier this year was listed for $10,750,000, but the court appointed receiver has now been discharged.

An 18-hole golf facility on more than 64 acres, the operation, on the south side of Ladner Trunk Road, just east of Highway 91 and north of Highway 99, had gone through financial woes.

The site is designated in Delta’s OCP as Agricultural/Conservation and Leisure.

items._ogDesc: Canadian household debt hit $3.29T in July as mortgage growth fell to one of the lowest rates in a generation & distress borrowing climbed.
items.body:
Households are on a borrowing spree, but mortgages are no longer the weapon of choice. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows household credit hit a new high in July. Mortgages continue to represent the lion’s share of debt, but growth is slowing to one of the weakest levels in a generation. Meanwhile, consumer debt continues to outpace mortgages, but for all the wrong reasons.

Canadian Household Total Credit Liabilities Reach $3.29 Trillion

Canadian household debt: total outstanding credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadian household debt pushed 0.3% (+$10.0 billion) higher to $3.29 trillion in July, 4.2% (+$131.4 billion) higher than last year. As mentioned, most of it’s still mortgage debt. However, its share is shrinking after consumer credit suddenly made a comeback.

Canadian Mortgage Debt Is Slowing To Unusually Low Levels

Canadian household debt: residential mortgage credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Mortgage debt is cooling, but still growing. The outstanding balance climbed 0.4% (+$8.7 billion) to $2.45 trillion in July, 4.0% (+$93.7 billion) higher than last year. Nearly 4% growth would be considered healthy for a balance this large, but it’s an anomaly for Canada. Over the past 27 years, only 17 months have seen growth at this level or lower. All of those months were in 2023 and 2024, during the recent correction.

Canadian Households Are Tapping Consumer Credit

Canadian household debt: consumer (non-mortgage) credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Consumer (non-mortgage) credit climbed 0.2% (+$1.3 billion) to $835.7 billion in July, up 4.7% (+$37.6 billion) since last year. The growth rate remains higher than mortgages, and this isn’t one of those good consumer growth surges.

The recent consumer credit bump is due to consumption smoothing and/or distress borrowing, according to TransUnion. Smoothing occurs when households use debt to avoid cutting expenses when their incomes fail to keep up. The credit agency warns that households are tapping higher-interest revolving credit to absorb the higher cost of living. TransUnion also found that mortgages were rising under similar circumstances, as balances are climbing on existing accounts, not new borrowing.

items._ogDesc: This week’s top stories are Canadian real estate’s slum pushes the demand balance to a 29 year low, and mortgage rates are about to rise.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada’s Plan To Fix Housing? Just Change What Affordable Means

Back in 2023, the CMHC said that building 3.5 million homes could restore 2004 levels of affordability by 2030. It reiterated the plan a year later, right before the country’s population growth plunged to nearly zero. Combined with the building boom, the bar should have been lower to achieve this goal by 2030. However, the agency’s latest report ignores its previous statement, moving the goalposts. The CMHC now expects affordability will be restored to 2019 levels if roughly 4.4 million homes are built by 2036. If you’re skeptical of the agency’s math, you should be. Here’s a brief overview of why.

Canadian Mortgage Rate Relief Done For This Stage of The Cycle: BMO

One of Canada’s largest banks doesn’t see much relief when it comes to mortgages in the near future. BMO Capital Markets warned the market is now pricing in five rate hikes from the Bank of Canada by the end of 2027. While BMO thinks that may be excessive based on its current read, rate hikes are coming. Mortgages are at cycle low, with hikes expected to throttle home sales in the coming weeks.

Canadian Real Estate Prices Fall, Demand Balance Hits 29-Year Low

The price of a typical home across Canada fell 0.7% to $657,500 in August, marking the third straight monthly drop. The drop was expected with sticky inventory and home sales falling 6.9% to the weakest August since 2012. The combination pushed the demand balance to its lowest level in 29 years. Canada’s housing recovery has barely started, and it’s already facing headwinds.

Canadian Inflation Stalled at 3%, But It’s Higher In All But Two Provinces

The Bank of Canada was lucky enough to see annual growth of CPI stall at 3.0% in August, but most Canadians aren’t that lucky. Only two provinces reported CPI growth at or below 3.0%: BC (+3.0%) and Ontario (+2.4%). Everywhere else came in much higher, especially in Atlantic Canada. The highest price growth was in Nova Scotia (+5.1%), where prices are rising at more than twice the Bank of Canada’s 2.0% target rate.

items.title: Municipalities demand B.C. to optimize industrial lands amid U.S. tariff pressures
items.description: UBCM members say industrial land is critical as businesses diversify markets and seek to boost domestic production
items._ogDesc: UBCM members say industrial land is critical as businesses diversify markets and seek to boost domestic production
items.body:
Municipalities across B.C. are asking the province to take action to protect and optimize industrial lands as U.S. tariff highlight the importance of “Made in Canada” products.

The majority of mayor and councillors voted in favour of a resolution to protect and optimize industrial lands in the province at the 2026 Union of B.C. Municipalities convention in Vancouver Friday.

Following the vote, UBCM will put the resolution forward for the province’s consideration.

“We've got generational procurement opportunities right now across the province, nationally and internationally, as we look to diversify markets [away from the U.S.],” said Jason Lum, councillor with the City of Chilliwack and a director at the Fraser Valley Regional District (FVRD), who submitted the motion.

“Whether it be in food processing, in defence, in advanced manufacturing, all of these things require a robust industrial land base.”

Industrial land has been dwindling with only a 10- to 15-year supply remaining in B.C., Lum said. The opportunities to add more land are limited.

He said there are few policies supporting the growth of industrial land and, in some cases, industrial land is being consumed by non-industrial uses. But industrial lands are essential to ensuring a vibrant local economy and providing jobs.

“The province is looking at their Buy BC program, but in order to buy B.C., we need to focus on those sectors that are actively building, creating, manufacturing the goods and producing the goods that we consume,” Lum said.

FVRD and many UBCM members want the province to recognize the importance of industrial lands and provide support to local governments to incentivize its protection. They are also calling for the identification of opportunities to expand the industrial land base.

For example, this could include identifying “brownfield” redevelopment opportunities - sites that have sat vacant and derelict for years - and helping to clean up and redevelop those sites to add more industrial land to the inventory, according to Lum.

“We need to act now, not just to protect and preserve, but also to unlock the incredible potential that we have right now with these generational opportunities that are sitting before us,” said Lum.

items.title: Semi-Complete Lake Simcoe 'Hedge Road Landing' Placed Under Creditor Protection
items.description:
The sprawling Hedge Road Landing subdivision project in Georgina, Ontario near Lake Simcoe has been placed under creditor protection midway through construction, according to Ontario Superior Court.

The project is planned to consist of three phases. Phase One is located at 6213 Black River Road, and includes 144 cottage-style bungalow homes. According to court documents, 75 units have been completed and sold, 24 units are under construction with 23 pre-sold, and 45 units have yet to commence construction with 13 pre-sold. The remaining two phases are set for vacant land nearby, and are set to include 168 units along the waterfront of Lake Simcoe.

The development website describes the project as an “adult active lifestyle community” with bungalows starting from the low $820,000s “to qualified purchasers,” and several units are listed on the website.

The project is held under 2055226 Ontario Inc. and is beneficially owned by three parties: Alliance (Sutton) Inc., Berkstar Developments Inc., and Rose Sutton Limited Partnership. Each owns a 33.33% interest, according to court documents, with Alliance Homes serving as the construction manager.

For the project, the developers obtained financing from Waterloo-based non-bank real estate lender MarshallZehr, which provided one loan in the principal amount of $48,553,000 for Phase One and another loan in the principal amount of $16,050,000 for the remaining two phases.

The Insolvency

The two loans matured on January 1 and March 1, 2026, respectively, and both were not repaid, with MarshallZehr owed a combined $42,907,636.19 as of August 13, and interest continuing to accrue.

According to MarshallZehr, the developers have also failed to keep up with payments to various contractors and suppliers, and seven liens totalling $5.7 million have been registered against the Phase One property since February.

“Construction Liens have created a significant impediment to the recommencement of construction activities at the Project and construction continues to be delayed,” said the court-appointed Monitor in a report submitted along with MarshallZehr’s creditor protection application. “Construction activities have largely ceased since April 2026. In the Proposed Monitor's view, continued delay in the recommencement of construction increases costs, delays home completions and closings, and may adversely affect the value of the Project.”

An overview of Hedge Road Landing. (Alliance Homes)

In an affidavit dated August 17, Alliance Homes’ President Alex Troop attributed the challenges the project has faced to the market downturn impacting liquidity, which then resulted in construction slowing down — a common sequence of events in this current cycle of insolvencies.

“205 [the ownership entity] has unfortunately been seriously impacted by the downturn in the GTA real estate market, demonstrated both by reduction in land values and a reduction in new home sales,” said Troop. “205 has not sold a new home since January of 2025, which has impacted cash flow and the ability to pay for construction of units already under contract to be sold. As a result, 205’s last closing of a house sale was on March 31, 2026.”

According to Troop, some purchasers have raised their concerns to the Home Construction Regulatory Authority (HCRA) and the HCRA’s review of those concerns is ongoing. Troop said he is also concerned that warranty provider Tarion may take action that could be detrimental to the project. He also said he has personally been advancing funds towards the project — $600,000 — but is unable to continue doing so.

Creditor Protection

The Ontario Superior Court granted MarshallZehr’s application on August 24 and the Hedge Road Landing project was placed under creditor protection, as defined under the federal Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA).

The goal of the proceeding is to put a pause on the various enforcement actions against the project, so the project can be completed.

There are now 10 units in Phase One set to be completed within the next three months that have been pre-sold. According to the Monitor, they retained Daniel Foch of Valery Real Estate (and a STOREYS contributor) to get an opinion on the value of the units, and Foch concluded that price increases of 5% to 10% could potentially be achieved if the units are remarketed (if the presales are terminated), but the Monitor says the assessment “does not take into consideration any negative stigma associated with the CCAA Proceedings, the cost to carry the homes for the staged listing period suggested, the cost and litigation risk in disclaiming the Existing APAs.”

The Monitor thus opted to carry on with the existing presale agreements in place and submitted an application outlining a process to complete the remaining sales that was approved by the court on August 28.

Creditor protection applications are usually granteed for an initial period of 10 days, after which extensions can be obtained upon application as needed. After Hedge Road Landing was placed under creditor protection on August 24, the stay of proceedings has now been extended to November 13, 2026, by which we should get the next update.
